name_swap: Hebrew 'שִׁמְעוֹן' is Simeon, but Chinese renders '西門' (Simon/Ximen), a different name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תַּאֲוַת גִּבְעֹת עוֹלָם' means 'the desire of the everlasting hills' (i.e., the choicest blessings of the ancient hills), but the Chinese renders it as '永遠小山丘的情慾' ('the lust of the everlasting hills'), which changes the meaning from a positive blessing to a negative or sexual connotation, altering the verse's claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'to the land of Canaan' (אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן), but the Chinese renders it as '由迦南人之地' (from the land of Canaan), reversing the direction. The sons carried him to Canaan, not from it.

name_swap: The Hebrew lists the personal names 'Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah' (רְאוּבֵן שִׁמְעוֹן לֵוִי וִיהוּדָה). The Chinese renders 'Reuben' as '流便支派' (the tribe of Reuben), adding '支派' (tribe) which is not in the Hebrew, and 'Simeon' as '西門' (correct), 'Levi' as '利未人' (the Levites/people of Levi), adding '人' (people) which is not in the Hebrew. These additions change the referents from individuals to tribal/group entities, which is a substantive difference in meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְּפָרֶךְ' means 'with harshness/rigor' (referring to the harshness of the work imposed on the Israelites), but the Chinese renders it as '以殘酷對待活物' ('treating living creatures cruelly'), which adds the concept of 'living creatures' (活物) not present in the Hebrew and shifts the meaning from harsh labor to cruelty toward animals/beings.
name_swap: The Hebrew name צִפֹּרָה (Zipporah) is rendered as 西比拉 (Sibila), which is a different name. The correct Chinese transliteration should be 西坡拉 or similar, not 西比拉.

name_swap: The Hebrew name צִפֹּרָה (Zipporah) is rendered as 西比拉 (Sibylla), which is a different name. The correct transliteration should be 西坡拉 or similar.; mistranslation: The Hebrew צֹר (flint) is rendered as 推羅 (Tyre), which is a place name, not the object used. The correct rendering should be 火石 or 石刀.; mistranslation: The Hebrew לְרַגְלָיו (to his feet) is rendered as 他的腳掌 (the sole of his foot), which narrows the meaning. The Hebrew refers to the feet generally, not specifically the sole.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לִלְבֹּן הַלְּבֵנִים' means 'to make bricks' (לְבֵנִים = bricks), but the Chinese renders it as '製作磚壇' (making brick altars), adding '壇' (altar) which is not in the Hebrew. This changes the meaning from making bricks to making brick altars.

mistranslation: The Hebrew has two distinct terms: אֹתֹתַי ('my signs') and מוֹפְתַי ('my wonders/portents'). The Chinese renders both as '神蹟' (signs/miracles), collapsing the distinction. While this is a lexical choice, it loses the second distinct concept 'wonders' and could mislead a reader into thinking only one category is mentioned twice.

addition: The Chinese adds '溪水也必變為血' (the stream water will also become blood), which is not present in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew only states that the fish will die and the river will stink (וּבָאַשׁ הַיְאֹר), not that it becomes blood.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּבָאַשׁ הַיְאֹר' means 'and the river stank' or 'became foul', but the Chinese renders it as '變為血' (became blood), which is a different concept not in this verse.; omission: The Hebrew 'וְנִלְאוּ מִצְרַיִם לִשְׁתּוֹת מַיִם מִן הַיְאֹר' means 'and the Egyptians were weary/loathed to drink water from the river' — the Chinese says '因渴而無法' (because of thirst, unable), which adds the cause '因渴' (because of thirst) not in the Hebrew, and changes the nuance from 'loathed/weary' to 'unable'.

omission: The Hebrew 'וַיִּמָּלֵא שִׁבְעַת יָמִים' (and seven days were fulfilled/completed) is rendered as '過了七日' (after seven days passed), which conveys the idea of seven days elapsing, but the verb 'מָלֵא' (was filled/completed) is not explicitly represented; however, the Chinese phrase '過了' (passed) is a close idiomatic rendering. The main issue is the omission of the subject 'הַיְאֹר' (the Nile/river) in the Chinese translation. The Hebrew states 'after Yahweh struck the Nile' (אַחֲרֵי הַכּוֹת יְהוָה אֶת הַיְאֹר), but the Chinese says '耶和華擊打溪之後' (after Yahweh struck the stream), dropping the definite object 'the Nile' and replacing it with '溪' (stream), which is a different noun and loses the specific reference to the Nile.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'חֳמָרִם חֳמָרִם' means 'heaps upon heaps' (piles of frogs, from context), not '土塊' (clods of earth). The Chinese renders it as '土塊' (soil clods), which is a mistranslation of the noun; it should be '堆' or '堆積' (heaps/piles).
mistranslation: Hebrew עָרֹב means 'swarms of flies' (or a mixed swarm), not '蝗蟲' (locusts). This changes the specific plague described.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְשָׁלִשִׁם עַל כֻּלּוֹ' means 'and officers over all of it' (i.e., officers over all the chariots), not 'three men on each chariot'. The Chinese rendering '每輛戰車上的三個人' (three men on each chariot) misinterprets 'שָׁלִשִׁם' (officers/third-men) as a numeral 'three' and changes the meaning.

addition: The Chinese adds '祂施行了拯救' (He performed salvation/deliverance), which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew ends with 'because in the matter in which they acted arrogantly against them' (כִּי בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם), with no mention of salvation or deliverance.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְהוֹדַעְתִּי אֶת חֻקֵּי הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֶת תּוֹרֹתָיו' means 'and I will make known the statutes of God and His laws' — the statutes and laws belong to God (אֱלֹהִים). The Chinese renders '神的律法和我的律例' ('God's laws and my statutes'), incorrectly attributing the statutes (חֻקֵּי) to the speaker ('my') instead of to God. This changes the ownership of the statutes.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'men fight' (אֲנָשִׁים, plural men) and one strikes a pregnant woman; the Chinese says 'two men fight' (兩個人爭鬥) and 'struck a pregnant wife' (擊打了一個懷孕的妻子). The Chinese adds 'two' (兩個) which is not in the Hebrew, and changes 'men' (plural, indefinite) to 'two men'. Also, the Hebrew has 'her children come out' (וְיָצְאוּ יְלָדֶיהָ) — the Chinese says 'her children fall out' (她的兒女墜落), which is a minor semantic shift but acceptable. The main issue is the addition of 'two' and the change from 'men' to 'two men', which alters the scenario.

addition: The Chinese adds '牛的主人須賠償' (the owner of the ox must compensate), but the Hebrew only says 'he shall give silver thirty shekels to his master' (יִתֵּן לַאדֹנָיו) — the subject is the owner of the ox implied, but the phrase '牛的主人' is an explicit addition not in the Hebrew; however, this is a natural clarification and does not change the meaning. More significantly, the Chinese says '給死者的主人' (to the master of the dead person), but the Hebrew says 'לַאדֹנָיו' (to his master) — the antecedent of 'his' is the slave or maidservant's master, not 'the dead person's master' — this is a mistranslation of the possessive pronoun, changing who receives the payment.

mistranslation: The Hebrew specifies 'five oxen' (חֲמִשָּׁה בָקָר) and 'four sheep' (אַרְבַּע צֹאן), but the Chinese renders '五對牲畜' (five pairs of livestock) and '四對羊群' (four pairs of flocks), adding '對' (pairs) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the number from five/four individual animals to five/four pairs, doubling the count.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'רְגָלִים' (regalim) means 'festivals' or 'pilgrimage festivals' (from the root רגל, 'to go on foot' or 'to celebrate a festival'), not '腳掌' (soles of the feet). The Chinese rendering '三次腳掌的節期' incorrectly translates 'רְגָלִים' as 'feet/soles' instead of 'festivals/pilgrimages', changing the meaning from 'three festivals' to 'three festivals of the soles of the feet'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' means 'tribes of Israel', but Chinese renders '以色列的十二個杖' ('twelve staffs of Israel'), which is a mistranslation of 'tribes' as 'staffs' (杖). This changes the meaning from tribal divisions to literal staffs.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַדֵּי' (poles/staves) is translated as '獨自' (alone/by oneself), which is a mistranslation. The correct meaning is 'poles' or 'staves' for carrying the ark/table. This changes the factual content.

mistranslation: Hebrew כַּפְתֹּרֶיהָ means 'its knobs/capitals' (ornamental knobs on the lampstand), but Chinese renders it as 門楣 ('lintel/door frame'), which is a different object not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'עֵבֶר פָּנֶיהָ' means 'the space in front of it' (i.e., the lampstand's front side), not '以巴衛的面' which appears to be a transliteration error or misreading; 'עֵבֶר' is 'side/region', not a proper name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase אִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחֹתָהּ means 'one to another' (literally 'a woman to her sister'), referring to the curtains being joined to each other. The Chinese renders it as '妻子連接於姊妹' (wife connected to sister), which introduces the concepts of 'wife' and 'sister' as literal persons, changing the meaning from curtains joined together to a familial relationship. This is a mistranslation that would mislead the reader.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'תַּחַת הַקְּרָסִים' means 'under the clasps/hooks' (referring to the clasps of the tabernacle curtains), but Chinese renders '放在帳棚之下' ('place under the tent'), which changes the location from under the clasps to under the tent, a substantive difference.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'קְלָעִים' means 'hangings/curtains', not '石塊' (stones). The Chinese adds a concept (stones) not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning of the item.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְרֹחַב חֲמִשִּׁים בַּחֲמִשִּׁים' means 'and the width fifty by fifty' (i.e., fifty cubits on each side, or a square of fifty), but the Chinese renders it as '寬是五十肘，又是五十肘' ('width is fifty cubits, and again fifty cubits'), which is a mistranslation of the distributive 'בַּחֲמִשִּׁים' (fifty by fifty). The Chinese adds an extra '又是五十肘' that misrepresents the Hebrew as stating the width twice rather than expressing a fifty-by-fifty dimension.

omission: The Hebrew states that the sound of the bells (קוֹלוֹ, 'his sound') will be heard when he comes into the holy place before YHWH and when he goes out. The Chinese rendering '他身上要穿著' ('he shall wear on himself') omits the explicit reference to the bells (the antecedent of 'his sound' in the Hebrew context, though the word 'bells' is not in this verse itself, the pronoun 'his' refers to the bells from the preceding context). More importantly, the Chinese adds '他身上要穿著' ('he shall wear on himself') which is not present in this verse; the Hebrew only says 'it shall be upon Aaron for ministering' (וְהָיָה עַל אַהֲרֹן לְשָׁרֵת), which the Chinese partially renders but then adds an extra clause about wearing. The Chinese also omits the explicit 'when he comes into the holy place before YHWH and when he goes out' (בְּבֹאוֹ אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ לִפְנֵי יְהוָה וּבְצֵאתוֹ) by compressing it into '進出聖所時' ('when going in and out of the sanctuary'), which loses the specific phrase 'before YHWH' (לִפְנֵי יְהוָה). The final clause '免得他死亡' ('lest he die') correctly renders וְלֹא יָמוּת, but the overall rendering adds an unstated action ('he shall wear') and omits the explicit 'before YHWH'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'קְטֹרֶת' means 'incense', not '乳香' (frankincense). Frankincense is 'לְבוֹנָה' in Hebrew. This changes the substance offered.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם' means 'for your generations' (i.e., throughout your generations), but the Chinese renders it as '作為你們世代的面' ('as the face of your generations'), which is a mistranslation. The word 'פָּנִים' (face) is not in the Hebrew here; the Hebrew has 'לִפְנֵי יְהוָה' ('before the LORD') earlier, but the final phrase is simply 'for your generations'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יִרְקַח' means 'to mix/compound (perfume/ointment)', not 'to shave hair'. The Chinese '剃髮' (shave hair) is a mistranslation. Also 'כָּמֹהוּ' means 'like it' (like the anointing oil), and 'יִתֵּן מִמֶּנּוּ עַל זָר' means 'puts any of it on a stranger/outsider', not 'gives him the shaved things'. The Chinese rendering changes the action from compounding the oil and applying it to a stranger to shaving hair and giving the shavings.

mistranslation: Hebrew קֹדֶשׁ הִוא לָכֶם means 'it is holy to you' (a holy day/thing), but Chinese renders it as '安息日是你們的聖所' ('the Sabbath is your sanctuary'), adding the concept of 'sanctuary/place' (聖所) not present in the Hebrew, which changes the meaning from 'holy' to a physical place.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says the tablets were the work of God (מַעֲשֵׂה אֱלֹהִים) and the writing was God's writing (מִכְתַּב אֱלֹהִים), but the Chinese renders '板的作為是神' which could be read as 'the work of the tablets is God' (reversing the construct relationship), and '書信是神的書信' adds '書信' (letter/epistle) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew has 'the writing' (הַמִּכְתָּב) not 'letter'. The phrase '書信是神的書信' is an awkward addition and misrepresents 'the writing is God's writing'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֶדְיוֹ' means 'his ornament/adornment' (generic jewelry or finery), but the Chinese renders it as '亞低' (a transliteration that looks like a proper name), which would mislead a reader into thinking it refers to a specific person or object named '亞低' rather than general ornaments.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'פֶּן תִּכְרֹת בְּרִית לְיוֹשֵׁב הָאָרֶץ' means 'lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land' (i.e., you, Israel, are the subject making the covenant). The Chinese '免得你所要到之地的居民與他們立約' reverses the subject and object, making the inhabitants the ones making a covenant with 'them' (a third party), which changes who is doing what to whom.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'קְטֹרֶת הַסַּמִּים' means 'incense of spices' (i.e., fragrant incense made of spices), but the Chinese renders it as '香料的乳香' (frankincense of spices). '乳香' specifically means 'frankincense' (levonah), which is not the same as 'incense' (ketoret). This changes the meaning from a general incense mixture to a specific substance.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַנְּשִׂאִם' means 'the leaders/princes' (נָשִׂיא), not '元帥' (military commander/general). This changes the identity of who brought the stones.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כַּפְתֹּרֶיהָ' means 'its knobs/capitals' (ornamental knobs), but the Chinese renders it as '門楣' (lintel/doorhead), which is a different concept not present in the Hebrew.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'קְלָעִים' means 'hangings/curtains' (woven screens), not '石塊' (stones). This changes the material described.
name_swap: Hebrew יָשְׁפֵה (yashfeh) is 'jasper' (碧玉/玉髓), not '雅各石' (Jacob stone). The Chinese rendering introduces a name not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew פַּאֲרֵי הַמִּגְבָּעֹת means 'the ornaments/headpieces of the turbans' (or 'the turbans' headpieces'), not '細麻頭巾的榮耀' ('the glory of the linen turbans'). The word פְּאֵר (pa'er) means 'headpiece/ornament/turban', not 'glory' (which would be כָּבוֹד). This changes the meaning of the item described.
addition: The Chinese adds '取水' (take water) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew only says 'wash from it' (וְרָחֲצוּ מִמֶּנּוּ), meaning 'wash from it' (the basin), not 'take water from it'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל' means 'crushed fresh grain' (or 'groats of fresh grain'), not '迦密山的麥子' (wheat from Mount Carmel). 'כַּרְמֶל' here is a common noun meaning 'fresh/ripe grain', not the proper name Carmel. This changes the meaning from a description of the grain's condition to a geographical location.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְּנֵי יוֹנָה' means 'young pigeons' (sons of a dove), but Chinese renders it as '鴿子的兒子' (sons of pigeons), which is a literal but awkward rendering; however, the meaning is preserved as 'young pigeons' in context. The issue is that 'תֹרִים' (turtledoves) is translated as '鴿子' (pigeons/doves), which is a different bird species; Hebrew distinguishes 'turtledoves' (תֹרִים) from 'pigeons' (יוֹנָה). This is a mistranslation of a specific animal name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְנֵי יוֹנָה' means 'young pigeons' (literally 'sons of a dove'), but the Chinese renders it as '兩隻鴿子的兒子' ('sons of two pigeons'), which misidentifies the referent: the Hebrew has 'two young pigeons' (two birds that are young doves), not 'sons of two pigeons' (offspring of two pigeons). This changes the meaning of the sacrificial animal.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֵגֶל' means 'calf', but the Chinese renders it as '公牛' (bull/ox). This changes the animal from a young calf to a full-grown bull.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְכָל מַשְׁקֶה' means 'and every drink' or 'and all drink' (referring to any beverage), but the Chinese renders it as '一切酒政' which means 'all wine officials' or 'all wine administration' — this is a mistranslation of the noun 'מַשְׁקֶה' (drink/beverage) as '酒政' (wine official), changing the meaning from a substance to a person/office.

mistranslation: Hebrew כֵּהָה means 'faded/dimmed/dulled', but Chinese renders it as 發白 ('turned white'), which is a different condition. The Hebrew says the lesion has faded, not that it has become white.
omission: The Hebrew specifies 'three tenths' (וּשְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה עֶשְׂרֹנִ֗ים) of fine flour for the grain offering, but the Chinese renders it as '十分之一' (one tenth), omitting the number three.

omission: The Hebrew text says 'after the death of Aaron's two sons' (אַחֲרֵי מוֹת שְׁנֵי בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן), but the Chinese renders it as '就在亞倫兩個兒子近到耶和前面之後' (after Aaron's two sons came near before Yahweh), omitting the word 'death' (מוֹת) and thus changing the meaning from 'after their death' to 'after they came near'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לַעֲזָאזֵל' (for Azazel) is rendered as '歸與贖罪羊' (belonging to the scapegoat), which misidentifies Azazel as the scapegoat. Azazel is a proper name (likely a demonic being or place), not the scapegoat itself. The Chinese translation incorrectly equates Azazel with the scapegoat, changing the meaning of the verse.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בִּגְדֵ֣י הַבָּ֔ד' means 'the linen garments' (בַּד = linen), but the Chinese renders it as '獨自衣服' ('alone/private clothes'), which is a mistranslation of the word 'בַּד' (linen) as if it were 'בָּדָד' (alone). This changes the meaning of the garments described.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'וְלֹא תַעֲשׂוּ מִכֹּל הַתּוֹעֵבֹת הָאֵלֶּה הָאֶזְרָח וְהַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכְכֶם' means 'and you shall not do any of these abominations, the native and the sojourner who sojourns among you' — i.e., both the native and the resident alien are the subjects who must not do these abominations. The Chinese rendering '不可在你們中間的土生人和寄居者中行一切可憎之物' ('do not do all abominations among the native-born and sojourners among you') makes the native and sojourner the location/object ('among them') rather than the subjects who are forbidden to act, thereby changing who is doing what. The Hebrew explicitly includes both groups as the ones who must not commit these acts, but the Chinese implies the acts are done 'among' them, altering the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'אוֹ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר תֵּצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת זָרַע' means 'or a man from whom an emission of semen goes out' (i.e., a man with a seminal emission, a bodily discharge, not '行淫' which means 'sexual immorality/fornication'). The Chinese '行淫' adds a moral/sexual-sin connotation not present in the Hebrew, which is a neutral ritual impurity term. This changes the meaning for a Chinese reader.; omission: The Hebrew 'וְהַנֹּגֵעַ בְּכָל טְמֵא נֶפֶשׁ' is rendered as '凡觸摸一切不潔性命的' which is acceptable, but the final clause 'לֹא יֹאכַל' (shall not eat) is implied in the Chinese '都不可吃聖所的物' — this is fine. However, the phrase 'אוֹ אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר תֵּצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת זָרַע' is rendered as '或是那有人行淫後裔從他而出的人' — '後裔' (offspring/descendant) is an addition; the Hebrew says 'emission of semen' (שִׁכְבַת זָרַע), not 'offspring'. This adds a concept not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'נֶפֶשׁ קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ' means 'a person bought with his money' (a slave purchased as property), not '買了性命作財物' (bought a life as property). The Chinese rendering '買了性命' (bought a life) misrepresents the object: it is a person/slave, not an abstract 'life'. This changes the meaning from purchasing a slave to purchasing a life.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'קֹדֶשׁ' (qodesh) means 'holy thing' or 'sacred offering', not '聖所' (sanctuary/holy place). The Chinese renders it as a place rather than the consecrated item being eaten.
omission: The Hebrew specifies 'two tenths' (שְׁנֵי עֶשְׂרֹנִים) for each cake, but the Chinese says 'one tenth' (十分之一), omitting the number two.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'שֵׁן' means 'tooth', not 'ivory' (象牙). The Chinese renders 'tooth for tooth' as '以象牙償還象牙' (ivory for ivory), which changes the meaning of the lexeme.

mistranslation: The Hebrew has the king saying 'I adjure you' (מַשְׁבִּיעֶךָ) — the king is making the prophet swear, not the king swearing by the LORD's name. name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel' (יוֹאָשׁ בֶּן יְהוֹאָחָז מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל), but the Chinese renders it as '以色列王約雅敬的兒子約阿施' (Joash son of Jehoiakim king of Israel). mistranslation: Hebrew says Uzziah was 16 years old (שֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה) when he began to reign, but Chinese says 十二歲 (12 years old).

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'מַעֲשֵׂיָהוּ' (Maaseiah) as the second officer, but the Chinese renders it as '瑪西雅' (Ma Xiya), which is a different name. name_swap: The Hebrew has 'בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ' (Beth-shemesh), but the Chinese renders it as '別是梅沙城' which appears to be a conflation or misrendering of 'Beth-shemesh' (בית שמש) with 'Beersheba' (באר שבע). The correct rendering should be '伯示麥' or similar, not '別是梅沙'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'וְכִפְרֹץ הַדָּבָר' means 'and when the matter spread' or 'and as the word spread' (referring to the proclamation about the tithe), but the Chinese renders it as '他們違背那話' ('they violated/transgressed that word'), which reverses the meaning. name_swap: The Hebrew has 'וְשִׁמְעִ֣י אָחִ֔יו' = 'and Shimei his brother', but the Chinese renders 'שִׁמְעִ֣י' as '希瑪利' (Himari?) which is not a standard transliteration of Shimei (示每/希每). name_swap: The Hebrew text begins with 'וְקוֹרֵא' (and Kore), a proper name, but the Chinese renders it as '可拉' (Korah). These are different names; Kore is the person in view, not Korah.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'וַיִּזְעֲקוּ הַשָּׁמָיִם' — 'they cried out to heaven' (the verb is plural, subject is Hezekiah and Isaiah). mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'אֶת רֶגֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעַל הָאֲדָמָה אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱמַדְתִּי לַאֲבֹתֵיכֶם' means 'the foot of Israel from the land which I have appointed for your fathers' — the land is appointed for the fathers, not 'from the land established by your fathers' (從你們父所立的田地). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הָאֲשֵׁרִים' refers to Asherah poles (wooden cultic objects), not '樹林' (forests/groves). The Chinese rendering '樹林' misrepresents the meaning.
name_swap: The Hebrew name אָמוֹן (Amon) is rendered as '亞捫人' (Ammonite), which changes the person's name to an ethnic designation. The correct rendering should be '亞捫' (Amon), not '亞捫人'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַבְּעָלִים' (the Baals) is rendered as '主人的' (the master's), which changes the referent from the pagan deity Baal to a generic 'master'. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וַיִּשְׁלַח ... עֲלֵיהֶם בְּיַד מַלְאָכָיו' means 'He sent [word] to them by His messengers' (i.e., He sent prophets/messengers to them), but the Chinese '藉著自己的天使屢次伸手差遣他們' renders '祂藉著自己的天使差遣他們' — making the messengers the agents who are sent, and '他們' (them) the object of sending, which reverses the direction: in Hebrew, the messengers are the means by which YHWH sends to the people (the people are the recipients, not the ones sent). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִֽי בָכֶ֣ם מִכָּל עַמּ֗וֹ' means 'Whoever among you of all his people' (i.e., 'anyone among you who belongs to his people'), but the Chinese renders it as '誰是他們中一切百姓' ('Who is among them all the people'), which misidentifies the subject and loses the sense of 'among you' and 'his people'.

name_swap: The Hebrew proper name בִגְוָי (Bigvai) is rendered as '大衛雅人' (people of David/Yah?), which is not a transliteration of Bigvai and introduces an incorrect name/ethnic descriptor not present in the Hebrew.

name_swap: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּנֵי עֵילָם אַחֵר' means 'the sons of Elam, another' (i.e., another Elam, a different group), but the Chinese renders '以攔人的兒子亞設爾' which introduces the name '亞設爾' (Asher?) not present in the Hebrew, and misrepresents 'אַחֵר' (another) as a personal name.

name_swap: Hebrew 'בְּנֵי אִמֵּר' means 'sons of Immer' (a priestly family name), but Chinese renders it as '以末利的兒子' ('sons of Yimoli'), which swaps the name 'Immer' for a different name 'Yimoli' (以末利). The correct transliteration should be '音麥' or similar for 'Immer'.

name_swap: The Hebrew name 'הַתִּרְשָׁתָא' (ha-Tirshata, the governor) is rendered as '提斯他' (Tisita), which is not a standard transliteration of 'Tirshata' and could be confused with a different name. The expected rendering would be '提斯哈他' or similar.
mistranslation: Hebrew פִּרְדֵיהֶם means 'their mules', but Chinese renders it as '他們的驢子' (their donkeys). This is a different animal and changes the factual content.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase בְּנֵי הַגּוֹלָה means 'the sons of the exile' (i.e., the returned exiles), but the Chinese renders it as '擄掠物的兒子' ('sons of the plunder/loot'), which misrepresents the meaning. 'הַגּוֹלָה' refers to the exile/captivity, not plunder.
addition: The Chinese adds '你們的神的殿' (the temple of your God) but the Hebrew only says 'we will build with you' (נִבְנֶה עִמָּכֶם) without specifying 'the temple of your God' in this clause.

name_swap: The Hebrew has two names: רְחוּם (Rehum) and שִׁמְשַׁי (Shimshai). The Chinese renders Rehum as 利宏 (correct) but renders Shimshai as 希實米人, which is a name swap/error — 希實米人 is not a transliteration of Shimshai; it appears to be a different name or a misreading. mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בַּעֲבַר נַהֲרָא' means 'beyond the river' (i.e., the region across the Euphrates), but the Chinese renders it as '過河處' ('the crossing place of the river'), which changes the meaning from a region to a specific location. name_swap: The Hebrew has 'שִׁמְשַׁי סָפְרָא' (Shimshai the scribe), but the Chinese renders '希實米人書記官' which appears to be a different name ('希實米' is not Shimshai). mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּכֹל עֲבַר נַהֲרָה' means 'over all the region beyond the River' (i.e., the province Beyond the River, a specific administrative region), not '在一切過河處' ('at all crossing places of the river'). name_swap: The Hebrew has 'שִׁמְשַׁי' (Shimshai), but the Chinese renders it as '希實米人' (Hishimi?), which appears to be a different name or a corruption. The correct transliteration should be '申示' or similar for Shimshai.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'פַּחַת עֲבַֽר נַהֲרָה' means 'governor of Beyond-the-River' (a specific official title), but the Chinese renders it as '百夫長' (centurion/commander of a hundred), which is a different concept and changes the official's title.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'פַּחַת עֲבַֽר נַהֲרָה' means 'governor of Beyond-the-River' (a title/office), but the Chinese renders it as '過河處河的百夫長' ('centurion of the river-crossing place'), which misidentifies the office as a military rank and mistranslates the geographic name.; name_swap: The Hebrew has 'תַּתְּנַי' (Tattenai) as the sender, but the Chinese renders it as '他特乃' (a transposition of characters, effectively a different name).; name_swap: The Hebrew has 'שְׁתַר בּוֹזְנַי' (Shethar-bozenai), but the Chinese renders it as '示他博斯乃' (a transposition of '示他' and '博斯乃', effectively swapping the order of the two names).; omission: The Hebrew 'וּכְנָוָתֵהּ' means 'and their associates/colleagues', but the Chinese renders it as '及其同伴' which is acceptable; however, the Hebrew 'אֲפַרְסְכָיֵא' (the Apharsachites) is rendered as '亞法薩迦' which is a transliteration but the Hebrew also includes 'דִּי בַּעֲבַ֣ר נַהֲרָה' ('who were in Beyond-the-River') which is omitted in the Chinese.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'דִּי אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא וְאַרְעָא' means 'of the God of heaven and earth' (God of heaven and earth), but the Chinese renders it as '天穹與地底之神' (God of the sky and the underworld), which changes the meaning: 'שְׁמַיָּא' is 'heaven(s)' and 'אַרְעָא' is 'earth', not '地底' (underworld). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כסדיא' (Chaldeans) is a separate noun referring to the Chaldeans, but the Chinese renders it as '迦勒底人' and attaches it to the delivery ('將迦勒底人與此家交付'), implying the Chaldeans were handed over along with the house. The Chinese misplaces '迦勒底人' as an object of the verb, changing who/what was handed over.

omission: The Hebrew text states that Cyrus the king issued a decree (שָׂם טְעֵם) to rebuild this house of God, but the Chinese adds '准許' (permitted/allowed), which is an addition not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew simply says he 'issued a decree' to rebuild, not that he 'permitted' it. This addition changes the nuance from a direct command/decree to a permission.

The Hebrew subject is 'the eye of my beholder' (עֵין רֹאִי), not 'my eye' (我的眼), and the verb is active ('will not see me'), not passive. This changes who is doing what to whom.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יִשָּׂא בְשִׂיחִי מִשְׁכָּבִי' means 'my couch will carry/ bear my complaint' (i.e., my bed will take up my complaint), but the Chinese renders it as '我的言語必扶起我的床' ('my words will lift up my bed'), reversing the subject and object: the Hebrew subject is 'my couch/bed' (מִשְׁכָּבִי) and the object is 'my complaint' (שִׂיחִי), whereas the Chinese makes 'my words' the subject and 'my bed' the object. This changes who is doing what to whom.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לַחֶרֶס' (la-cheres) means 'to the sun' (חרס = sun), not 'to pottery/陶器'. The Chinese renders it as '陶器' (pottery), which is a mistranslation of the noun.

negation: The Hebrew 'וַֽיַּעֲנֵנִי' means 'and he answered me' (positive), but the Chinese renders it as '他卻不應允' ('he did not answer'), reversing the meaning. The Hebrew states 'If I call and he answers me, I would not believe that he listens to my voice' — the Chinese incorrectly negates the answering.

omission: The Hebrew 'לֹא יִתְּנֵנִי הָשֵׁב רוּחִי' means 'He will not let me return my spirit' (i.e., He will not allow me to recover/regain my breath/spirit), but the Chinese adds '交給陰間' (deliver to Sheol), which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has no mention of Sheol/陰間 here.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְּחַיָּי' means 'in my life' or 'while I live', not '活物' (living creatures). The Chinese mistranslates this as 'living creatures'.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'שִׂיחִי' means 'my complaint' or 'my meditation', not '我的言語' (my words/speech). The Chinese rendering changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שְׂבַע קָלוֹן וּרְאֵה עָנְיִי' means 'I am full of disgrace, and see my misery' (or 'be full of disgrace and see my affliction'), addressed to God as an imperative 'see' (רְאֵה). The Chinese renders '滿眼羞辱，求你看顧我的困苦人' which adds '求你看顧' (beg you to look after) and '困苦人' (afflicted person), introducing a third-person object ('my afflicted person') not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has 'עָנְיִי' = 'my affliction/misery' (first-person singular suffix), not '困苦人' (afflicted person). Also 'שְׂבַע' is 'full of' (adjective), not '滿眼' (full of eyes). The imperative 'רְאֵה' is 'see' (addressed to God), not '看顧' (look after/care for). This changes the meaning and adds an element not present.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וַתֹּפַע' (from יפע, 'to shine/beam forth') is rendered as '震動' (to shake/tremble), which changes the meaning. The verse says the land 'shines forth' like darkness, not that it trembles.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְעַיִר פֶּרֶא אָדָם יִוָּלֵד' means 'and a wild donkey's foal is born a man' (i.e., a person is born like a wild donkey's colt, implying foolishness). The Chinese '野驢的騾駒必被人所生' says 'the mule colt of a wild donkey will be born by a man,' which reverses the subject/object: in Hebrew, the man is born (as a wild donkey's colt), not the colt being born by a man. This changes who is born and the meaning.
mistranslation: The Hebrew verb יַהֲרוֹס means 'tear down' or 'destroy', but the Chinese renders it as '建造' (build), reversing the action. The correct rendering should be '拆毀' or '毀壞'.
mistranslation: Hebrew מֵסִיר means 'removes/takes away', but Chinese renders it as '賜予' (gives/bestows), reversing the action. The verse says God removes speech from the faithful, not gives it.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַחֲרֵשׁ תַּחֲרִישׁוּן' is an emphatic construction meaning 'you would indeed be silent' (from חָרַשׁ, 'to be silent'), not 'become deaf' (which would be חֵרֵשׁ, 'deaf'). The Chinese '成為聾子' (become deaf) misrepresents the verb as 'deaf' instead of 'silent'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'קָצִיר' means 'harvest' (a crop), not '收割者' (harvester/reaper). The Chinese adds '者' (person suffix), changing the meaning from the harvest itself to the person who harvests.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Eliphaz the Temanite' (אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י), but the Chinese renders '推羅人以利法斯' which means 'Eliphaz the Tyrian' (from Tyre/推羅), not 'the Temanite' (from Teman). This swaps the ethnic/geographic designation.

mistranslation: The Hebrew clause 'וְהֹצֵאתָ מִפִּיךָ מִלִּין' means 'and you bring forth words from your mouth' (i.e., you utter words), but the Chinese renders it as '你若將話語從你口中除去' ('if you remove words from your mouth'), reversing the action from bringing forth to removing. This changes the meaning of the verse.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בִּקְדֹּשָׁו' (in His holy ones) is rendered as '他們雖獻為聖' (though they are consecrated/offered as holy), which changes the subject from God's holy ones/angels to a human act of consecration. The Hebrew means 'even His holy ones He does not trust,' not 'they are consecrated but do not believe.'

mistranslation: Hebrew 'לְגַלִּים' (from גַּל, 'heap of ruins' or 'mound') is rendered as '波浪' (waves), which is a mistranslation. The phrase 'אֲשֶׁר הִתְעַתְּדוּ לְגַלִּים' means 'which they had prepared for heaps of ruins' (i.e., destined to become ruins), not 'prepared for waves'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אַחְבִּירָה עֲלֵיכֶם בְּמִלִּים' means 'I would join/string together words against you' (i.e., speak forcefully against you), not 'I would make a covenant with you in words' (立約). The verb חָבַר means 'to join/associate', not 'to covenant' (בְּרִית). This changes the meaning from adversarial speech to a covenant-making act.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְאָנִיעָה עֲלֵיכֶם בְּמוֹ רֹאשִׁי' means 'and I would shake my head at you' (a gesture of scorn/mockery), not 'and I swear by my head' (以我的頭起誓). The verb נוּעַ means 'to shake/move to and fro', not 'to swear'. This changes the gesture from derision to an oath.

omission: The Hebrew 'וַיְקִימֵנִי לוֹ לְמַטָּרָה' means 'He set me up as His target' (i.e., a mark for His arrows), but the Chinese renders it as '祂為我設立監獄' ('He established a prison for me'), which introduces the concept of a prison not present in the Hebrew and omits the meaning of being set as a target.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לַשַּׁחַת קָרָאתִי אָבִי אָתָּה אִמִּי וַאֲחֹתִי לָרִמָּה' means 'I called to the Pit: You are my father, my mother and my sister to the worm.' The Chinese adds '你們卻把我交給蟲子' ('but you handed me over to the worm'), which is an addition not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew does not say the Pit/worm handed the speaker over; rather, the speaker addresses the Pit as family. This addition changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְתִקְוָתִי מִי יְשׁוּרֶנָּה' means 'and my hope—who can see it?' (or 'who can behold it?'), not 'who can defend my hope?' The verb 'יְשׁוּרֶנָּה' (from שׁוּר, 'to see/behold') is rendered as '辯護' (defend), which changes the meaning from perception/visibility to advocacy.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'עַל יוֹמוֹ' means 'at his day' (i.e., at the day of his calamity), not 'in their daily [affairs]' (在他們的每日中). The Chinese rendering misconstrues the singular suffix and the temporal sense.; number_person_tense: Hebrew 'אַחֲרֹנִים' (latter ones) and 'קַדְמֹנִים' (former ones) are plural subjects; Chinese '後者' and '前者' are singular, changing the number.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'נָשַׁמּוּ' means 'are appalled/desolated' (from שׁמם), not 'are cut off' (斷絕). The Chinese adds a concept of cessation not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַיִן שְׁזָפַתּוּ' means 'the eye sees it' (or 'gazes upon it'), not 'the eye despises it' (輕視). The verb שָׁזַף means 'to see/gaze', not 'to despise'. This changes the meaning of the clause.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְלֹא תוֹסִיף' means 'and it will not add' (i.e., it will not continue to exist or be seen again), but the Chinese '不再加添' means 'no longer adds/increases', which misrepresents the subject and action. The subject is the eye or the thing seen, not an addition.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְלֹא עוֹד תְּשׁוּרֶנּוּ מְקוֹמוֹ' means 'and its place will no longer see it' (i.e., the place will not see it again), but the Chinese '也不再從其地方轉移它' means 'nor will it be moved from its place', reversing the subject-object relationship and adding the concept of 'moving' not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תַּהַרְגֵהוּ לְשׁוֹן אֶפְעֶה' means 'the tongue of the viper kills him' (i.e., the viper's tongue kills the person who drinks the head), but the Chinese renders it as 'his tongue will kill the viper' (他的舌頭要殺死毒蛇), reversing the subject and object. The subject of 'תַּהַרְגֵהוּ' is 'לְשׁוֹן אֶפְעֶה' (the tongue of the viper), and the object is 'הוּ' (him, the one drinking). The Chinese makes the person's tongue the subject and the viper the object, changing who does what to whom.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תַלְעִיג' (from לָעַג) means 'you may mock/deride', but the Chinese renders it as '你們就退去' ('you may withdraw/leave'), which changes the meaning from mocking to departing.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֶאָנֹכִי לְאָדָם שִׂיחִי' is a rhetorical question: 'Is my complaint to a man?' The Chinese renders it as a statement '我對人說話' (I speak to people), losing the interrogative and the nuance of 'complaint' (שִׂיחִי). Also, the second clause 'וְאִם מַדּוּעַ לֹא תִקְצַר רוּחִי' means 'and if so, why is my spirit not impatient?' (or 'why should my spirit not be short?' i.e., 'why should I not be impatient?'), but the Chinese '為何我的靈仍不發出' (why does my spirit still not emit?) misrepresents the verb 'תִקְצַר' (to be short/impatient) as '發出' (to emit), changing the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְּעֶצֶם תֻּמּוֹ' means 'in the very fullness/strength of his prosperity' (עֶצֶם = bone/strength/essence, תֻּמּוֹ = his completeness/prosperity), not 'in the completeness of his bones' (骸骨的完全). The Chinese renders 'עֶצֶם' as 'bones' (骸骨) rather than 'strength/essence', changing the meaning from dying in the midst of prosperity to dying in bodily completeness.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Eliphaz the Temanite' (אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י), but the Chinese renders '推羅人' (Tyrian/from Tyre), which is a different ethnic/geographic designation. The correct rendering should be '提幔人以利法' (Eliphaz the Temanite).

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַלְאֵ֥ל יִסְכָּן גָּ֑בֶר' means 'Can a man be profitable to God?' (i.e., 'Does a man benefit God?'), not 'Can a man be inhabited by God?' The verb 'יִסְכָּן' (from סכן) means 'to profit/benefit' or 'to be useful', not 'to dwell/inhabit'. The Chinese '為神所居住' (be inhabited by God) changes the meaning entirely. The second clause 'כִּֽי יִסְכֹּ֖ן עָלֵ֣ימוֹ מַשְׂכִּֽיל' means 'for a wise man benefits himself' (i.e., a wise man profits himself), not 'He will surely care for them' (祂必眷顧他們). The subject 'מַשְׂכִּיל' (wise man) is rendered as '祂' (He) referring to God, and 'עָלֵימוֹ' (upon himself/for himself) is mistranslated as 'them' (他們). This reverses the subject and object and changes the verse's claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְשִׁית עַל עָפָ֥ר בָּ֑צֶר וּבְצ֖וּר נְחָלִ֣ים אוֹפִֽיר' is a poetic line (Job 22:24) meaning 'and place [your] gold in the dust, and [the gold of] Ophir among the stones of the brooks.' The Chinese renders 'בָּצֶר' (gold, treasure) as '比色城' (a city name 'Bizeth'?), and 'אוֹפִיר' (Ophir, a place known for gold) as '俄斐' (Ophir) but misconstrues the syntax: the Hebrew has 'place gold on the dust' and 'Ophir [gold] among the stones of the brooks' — the Chinese says 'spread its dust on the city of Bizeth, and pile its valley's rocks into Ophir,' which reverses the imagery and adds a city name not in the text. The meaning is substantially altered.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יְמַלֵּט אִי נָקִי' means 'He will deliver the innocent man' (or 'the innocent island' as a rare word), but the Chinese renders it as a rhetorical question '他豈能救潔淨的人呢？' ('Can he save the clean/pure person?'), which reverses the meaning from a positive statement to a question implying inability. The Hebrew is a declarative statement, not a question.; mistranslation: The second clause 'וְנִמְלַט בְּבֹר כַּפֶּיךָ' means 'and he will be delivered by the purity of your hands' (i.e., through your clean hands), but the Chinese '他必從你的手掌中被救出' ('he will be rescued from your palm') changes the agent/instrument: the Hebrew says deliverance is through the purity of your hands, not from being taken out of your hand. This alters the meaning of who is doing what.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'גְּבֻלוֹת יַשִּׂיגוּ' means 'they reach/attain boundaries' (subject is 'they', i.e., the wicked), not 'their boundaries will expand'. The Chinese renders it as a passive/impersonal expansion of boundaries, changing the subject and action. The Hebrew has the wicked seizing boundaries, not boundaries expanding.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֵדֶר גָּזְלוּ וַיִּרְעוּ' means 'they stole a flock and pastured it' (subject 'they' continues), but the Chinese says '掠奪的羊群必來牧放' ('the plundered flock will come to graze'), making the flock the subject and adding '必來' (will come) which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has the wicked as the active agents of stealing and pasturing, not the flock acting.

addition: The Chinese adds '從母懷中' (from the mother's bosom), which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew says 'they seize the orphan from the breast' (מִשֹּׁד יָתוֹם), where 'שֹׁד' means 'breast' or 'bosom', but the Chinese rendering '從母懷中' explicitly adds 'mother' (母) which is not in the Hebrew text. This is a substantive addition that changes the imagery.
omission: The Hebrew 'וְהֻמְּכוּ' (and they are brought low/humbled) is not represented in the Chinese; the phrase '你們再尋找，他已不在' covers 'וְאֵינֶנּוּ' but the humbling/being brought low is missing.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'מִיָּמָי' means 'from my days' i.e. 'in all my days' / 'all my life', but Chinese '從我日中' reads as 'from my days' literally, which is awkward; more importantly, the Hebrew 'לֹא יֶחֱרַף לְבָבִי' means 'my heart will not reproach/taunt me' (i.e. my heart will not condemn me), but Chinese '我的心必不從我日中蒙羞' renders it as 'my heart will not be put to shame from my days', changing the subject/action: Hebrew has the heart as the agent of reproach, Chinese makes the heart the object of shame. This alters who is doing what.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לֹא אֲכַחֵד' means 'I will not conceal/hide' (from כחד), but the Chinese renders it as '我必不懼怕' ('I will not fear'), which changes the meaning from concealing to fearing.

addition: The Chinese adds '風' (wind) at the end, which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew 'בָּרוֹחַ יִבְרָח' means 'he will surely flee' (infinitive absolute + finite verb for emphasis), not 'flee from the wind'.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'מֶשֶׁךְ חָכְמָה' means 'the acquisition/possession of wisdom' (מֶשֶׁךְ = 'drawing out/acquiring', not a personal name). The Chinese renders it as '瑪士撒克的智慧' ('Methuselah's wisdom'), introducing a personal name (Methuselah) that is not in the Hebrew and changing the meaning from 'the getting of wisdom' to a specific person's wisdom.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שִׂיחִים' means 'shrubs/bushes' (or possibly 'broom bushes'), not '言語' (words/speech). The Chinese renders it as '言語之間' (among words), which is a mistranslation of the noun.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'פִּרְחַח' (from פָּרַח, 'to bud/flourish') refers to 'scoundrels' or 'base fellows' (literally 'blossoms' as a metaphor for worthless people), not '少年人' (youths). The Chinese rendering changes the meaning from 'worthless/scoundrel people' to 'young people'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'חלצו' (hiphil of חלץ, 'to rescue/deliver') is rendered as '以腰' ('with the waist/loins'), which is a misreading. The correct sense is 'if they have not been rescued/delivered' (referring to the poor/needy), not 'if they do not bless me with the waist.' This changes the meaning of the clause.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּמִשְּׂאֵתוֹ' means 'and from his exaltation/loftiness' (referring to God's majesty), but the Chinese renders it as '那驚恐的尊貴' ('that terrifying majesty'), adding '驚恐的' (terrifying) which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew phrase is simply 'his exaltation' without an adjective like 'terrifying'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וָאֶדֹּם' (from דמם) means 'I was silent/kept silent', not '我雖被染紅' ('though I was dyed red'). The Chinese mistranslates the verb, changing the meaning.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'לֹא אֵצֵא פָתַח' means 'I would not go out of the door' (i.e., I did not leave my door), not '卻不從門而出' which is acceptable, but the main issue is the preceding clause. The overall sense of silence/restraint is lost.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֵל יִדְּפֶנּוּ לֹא אִישׁ' means 'God will rebuke him, not a man' (or 'God will pursue him, not a man'), i.e., it is God, not a man, who will drive him away. The Chinese renders it as '人不能勝過他，連神也不能' ('man cannot overcome him, even God cannot'), which reverses the meaning: the Hebrew says God (not man) will do the action, while the Chinese says neither man nor God can overcome him. This changes the subject and negates the divine action.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לֹא יְשׁוּרֶנָּה' means 'he does not regard it' (i.e., God does not consider/observe it), but the Chinese renders it as '都不改變' (does not change), which changes the meaning. The subject of 'יְשׁוּרֶנָּה' is God, and the object is the matter spoken; the Chinese implies God's own unchangeableness, whereas the Hebrew says God does not look upon/regard the thing (or possibly 'he does not see it' in the sense of not repeating it). This is a substantive semantic shift.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'בַּשָּׁלַח' (ba-shalach) is a place name 'Shalach' (or 'the Shalach'), but the Chinese renders it as '沙拉' (Shala), which is a different transliteration. More importantly, the Hebrew 'מֵעֲבֹר בַּשָּׁלַח' means 'from passing over into the pit/Sheol' (or 'from crossing the river/stream'), not 'from passing through Shala' as a proper name. The Chinese adds a proper name '沙拉' that is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew 'שָׁלַח' here likely refers to 'the pit' or 'Sheol' (a common poetic term), not a place name. This changes the meaning: the verse says God keeps his life from passing into the pit, not from passing through a place called Shala.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַחֲרֵשׁ וַאֲאַלֶּפְךָ חָכְמָה' means 'be silent, and I will teach you wisdom' (an imperative to the listener to be silent, followed by the speaker's promise to teach). The Chinese renders it as '我就默然不語，不再以智慧教導你' ('I will be silent and no longer teach you wisdom'), reversing the subject/action: the Hebrew has the speaker commanding the listener to be silent and then offering to teach, whereas the Chinese has the speaker himself becoming silent and withholding teaching. This changes who is doing what and adds the negation '不再' (no longer) not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל מִשְׁפָּטִי אֲכַזֵּב' means 'I would lie against my judgment/right' (i.e., I would be false to my own cause), not '因我的審判，我必使他失敗' ('because of my judgment, I will cause him to fail'). The subject of 'אֲכַזֵּב' is the speaker, not an external 'him'.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אָנוּשׁ חִצִּי בְלִי פָשַׁע' means 'my arrow is incurable/desperate without transgression' (i.e., my wound is fatal though I am innocent), not '那無罪的，我卻以箭攻擊' ('the innocent one, I attack with arrows'). The phrase 'בְלִי פָשַׁע' modifies the speaker's condition, not an object being attacked.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְלֹא נִכַּר שׁוֹעַ לִפְנֵי דָל' means 'nor regards the noble more than the poor' (i.e., does not show favoritism to the rich over the poor). The Chinese '也不顧貧民的哀號' ('nor regards the cry of the poor') introduces '哀號' (cry/wailing) which is not in the Hebrew, and changes the meaning from not favoring the noble over the poor to ignoring the poor's cry. The Hebrew contrasts 'שָׂרִים' (princes/officials) and 'שׁוֹעַ' (noble) with 'דָל' (poor), not 'cry of the poor'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מַה יִּסְכָּן לָךְ' means 'What profit is it to you?' (i.e., what benefit does God gain from my righteousness), not '我當為你預備甚麼呢' ('What should I prepare for you?'). The verb 'יִּסְכָּן' means 'profit/gain', not 'prepare'. This changes the meaning of the verse.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מָה אֹעִיל מֵחַטָּאתִי' means 'What do I gain from my sin?' (i.e., what benefit do I get from my sin), not '從我的罪中我能獻甚麼呢' ('What can I offer from my sin?'). The verb 'אֹעִיל' means 'profit/gain', not 'offer/sacrifice'. negation: The Hebrew 'כִּי יְשֻׁבוּן מֵאָוֶן' means 'that they would turn back from iniquity' (positive: they will return from evil). mistranslation: Hebrew בִֽישִׁימ֣וֹן (biyshimon) means 'in the wilderness/desert' (בְּ + יְשִׁימוֹן), not '耶示崙' (Yeshurun). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יִדֹּדוּן יִדֹּדוּן' means 'they flee, they flee' (from the root נדד, 'to flee'), but the Chinese renders it as '必得賞賜' ('will surely receive reward'), which is a mistranslation. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'רִבֹּתַ֣יִם אַלְפֵ֣י שִׁנְאָ֑ן' means 'twice ten thousand, thousands of Shinan' (i.e., 'myriads, thousands of Shinan' – Shinan is a place name, likely referring to Sinai or a region). This changes the meaning: the Hebrew speaks of myriads and thousands of Shinan (a place), not of archangels.; name_swap: The Hebrew 'שִׁנְאָ֑ן' (Shinan) is a proper place name, but the Chinese translates it as part of a phrase '千個天使長' (thousands of archangels), effectively dropping the place name and substituting a different concept.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שִׁבֹּלֶת מַיִם' means 'flood of water' or 'torrent of water', not '耳麥的水' (water of earbuds/ears of grain). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְאֶל מַכְאוֹב חֲלָלֶיךָ יְסַפֵּרוּ' means 'and they recount the pain of your wounded' (i.e., they speak about the suffering of those you have wounded). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֹהֲבֵי יְשׁוּעָתֶךָ' means 'those who love Your salvation' (a noun phrase, subject of the verb 'יִגְדַּל'), but the Chinese renders it as '願喜愛你救恩的神' ('the God who loves Your salvation'), making God the subject of the blessing instead of the lovers of salvation. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אַתָּה גוֹזִי' means 'you are the one who drew me out' (from the womb), i.e., 'you are my deliverer/one who brought me forth'. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כִּי בֹ֥שׁוּ כִֽי חָ֝פְר֗וּ' means 'for they are ashamed, for they are confounded/dismayed' (both verbs expressing shame/confusion), but the Chinese renders it as '因羞愧而絆倒' ('stumble because of shame'), adding the concept of 'stumbling' (絆倒) which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has no verb for 'stumble' here; it only states that the seekers of my harm are ashamed and confounded.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'פִסַּת בַּר' means 'abundance of grain' (a measure/abundance of wheat), not 'a handful of wheat' (一把). This is a mistranslation of the subject and verb.
name_swap: The Hebrew 'דָּוִד בֶּן יִשָׁי' means 'David, son of Jesse' (David is the son of Jesse). The Chinese renders it as '大衛的兒子耶西' (Jesse, son of David), reversing the father-son relationship.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יוֹבִילוּ שַׁי לַמּוֹרָא' means 'they shall bring tribute to the One who is to be feared' (i.e., to God, the Awesome One). The phrase should convey 'to the Awesome One' (God), not 'to fear'.
addition: The Chinese adds '但我要追念' (but I will remember) which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew only states 'I said,

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וֶעֱזוּזוֹ' means 'and His might/strength' (abstract noun), but Chinese renders it as '祂的大能者' ('His mighty ones'), which changes the meaning from an attribute of God to persons. The correct rendering should be '祂的大能' or '祂的威能'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְיָשִׂימוּ בֵאלֹהִים כִּסְלָם' means 'and they put their trust/confidence in God' (כֶּסֶל = trust/confidence), but Chinese says '他們卻將愚昧歸於神' ('they attributed folly to God'), which reverses the meaning—the Hebrew says they trusted God, not that they blamed Him for folly.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הוֹתֵר' (from יָתַר, meaning 'spare' or 'preserve alive') is rendered as '保護' (protect), which changes the meaning. The verse asks God to spare/preserve those doomed to death, not merely protect them.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל אִישׁ יְמִינֶךָ' means 'upon the man of your right hand' (i.e., the man at your right hand), but the Chinese renders it as '在你右邊之人的手上' ('upon the hand of the man at your right hand'), adding '手上' (hand) which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has 'יָדְךָ' (your hand) as the subject, and 'עַל אִישׁ' (upon the man), not 'upon the hand of the man'.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ' means 'to the chief musician/choirmaster' (a title), but the Chinese renders it as '交革提他人' which appears to be a garbled transliteration of 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ' (perhaps confusing it with 'גתית' or another term). Additionally, the Hebrew 'לְאָסָף' is 'for Asaph' (a proper name), which the Chinese renders as '亞薩' correctly, but the overall phrase '交革提他人' is not a faithful rendering of 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ עַל הַגִּתִּית'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לַמְנַצֵּחַ' means 'for the choir director' or 'to the chief musician,' but the Chinese renders it as '交革提他人' (hand over to the Gittite), which misidentifies the addressee. The Chinese conflates these, changing the meaning.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִשְׁכְּנוֹתֶיךָ' means 'your dwellings' (plural), but the Chinese renders it as '你的軍隊的會幕' (your army's tabernacle), adding '軍隊' (army) which is not in the Hebrew. The phrase 'יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת' is 'YHWH of hosts' (a divine title), not 'your army's.' This changes the possessive and adds an unstated concept.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'לְאֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי' means 'for Ethan the Ezrahite' (a proper name), but the Chinese renders it as '屬亞薩拉喜人以探' which introduces '亞薩拉喜人' (Asa/Asaph? unclear) and misidentifies the person; the name 'Ethan' is present but the patronymic/gentilic is garbled and an extra name '亞薩' appears, changing the identity.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מֶה חָלֶד' means 'what is [my] life-span/mortality' (i.e., 'how fleeting is life'), but the Chinese renders it as '我這世代' ('this generation of mine'), which changes the meaning from a rhetorical question about the brevity of life to a reference to a specific generation. The Hebrew has no explicit 'why' word; the 'עַל מַה' is 'for what' (a purpose clause), not 'why'.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְּשׁוּרָי' means 'upon my enemies' (from שׁוּר, 'enemy'), not '書珥地' (a place name 'Shur'). The Chinese renders it as a geographical location, changing the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּמְלֹאוֹ' means 'and its fullness' (i.e., everything in the sea), but the Chinese '並充滿滿足' renders it as 'and be filled with satisfaction', adding a concept of satisfaction not present in the Hebrew and misrepresenting the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הוֹשִׁיעָה לּוֹ יְמִינוֹ וּזְרוֹעַ קָדְשׁוֹ' means 'His right hand and His holy arm have worked salvation for Him' (i.e., the LORD's own right hand and holy arm accomplished salvation for Him, not for others). The Chinese '祂的右邊和聖所的臂膀帶來了拯救' renders '祂的右邊' (His right side) instead of '祂的右手' (His right hand), and '聖所的臂膀' (the arm of the sanctuary) instead of '祂的聖臂' (His holy arm), changing the meaning from God's own holy arm to an arm associated with the sanctuary. mistranslation: Hebrew עֵדֹתָיו means 'his testimonies/statutes', not 'his congregation/會眾'. The Chinese '會眾' (congregation) is a mistranslation of the Hebrew word.

addition: The Chinese adds '作為樂歌者' (as a psalmist/song-singer), which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew only says 'come before His presence with joyful singing' (בִּרְנָנָה), not that the worshiper is a 'song-singer' or 'psalmist'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נַפְשִׁי' means 'my soul' or 'my being', not '大衛的性命' (David's life). The psalm is addressed by David, but the phrase is first-person 'my soul', not a third-person reference to David.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עֶדְיֵךְ' means 'your adornment/ornament' (from עדי), not a proper name '亞低'. The Chinese renders it as a transliterated name '亞低', which is a mistranslation. The phrase should be '以美物使你的裝飾滿足' or similar, meaning 'who satisfies your adornment with good things'.

name_swap: The Hebrew 'בִּישִׁימוֹן' (bishimon) means 'in the wasteland/desert' (a common noun), not the proper name '耶示崙' (Jeshurun). The Chinese renders it as a place name, which is a mistranslation of the common noun.

name_swap: Hebrew 'בִּישִׁימוֹן' (yeshimon, 'wasteland/desert') is rendered as '耶示崙' (Yeshurun), a different proper name not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew text has no proper name here; it is a common noun for a desolate place.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שֹׂטְנַי' means 'my adversaries' (plural, from the root שׂטן, 'to accuse/adversary'), not the proper name 'Satan' (撒但). The Chinese rendering '撒但' introduces a specific personal name not present in the Hebrew, changing the meaning from 'my adversaries' to 'Satan'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כְּצֵל כִּנְטוֹתוֹ נֶהֱלָכְתִּי' means 'I walk like a shadow when it lengthens' (i.e., as the shadow declines/extends), not '行在祂翅膀的陰影下' (walking under His wings' shadow). The phrase 'כִּנְטוֹתוֹ' refers to the shadow's stretching/declining, not God's wings. The Chinese adds '祂翅膀的' (His wings) which is not in the Hebrew, and misrepresents the subject of the shadow.; omission: The Hebrew 'נִנְעַרְתִּי' means 'I am shaken out' or 'I am driven away' (like a locust being shaken off), but the Chinese renders it as '顫抖' (trembling), which loses the sense of being shaken out/driven away. The comparison 'כָּאַרְבֶּה' (like the locust) is preserved, but the verb nuance is altered.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'אֶבְיוֹן' means 'needy/poor', not 'righteous' (義人). The Chinese renders '義人' which changes the identity of the person being helped.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה' means 'the beginning of wisdom' (i.e., the first/chief part of wisdom), not '起初智慧' ('in the beginning, wisdom'). The Chinese '一切行祂旨意的皆有智慧' ('all who do His will have wisdom') substitutes 'His will' for 'them' (referring to wisdom/fear) and changes 'good understanding' to 'wisdom', altering the object and the specific claim.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אַשְׁרֵי אִישׁ יָרֵא אֶת יְהוָה' means 'Blessed is the man who fears the LORD', but the Chinese renders it as '有福的人啊，要讚美耶和華' ('Blessed person, praise the LORD'), which changes the subject and adds an imperative to praise, misrepresenting the original as a blessing on the one who fears the LORD.

mistranslation: The Hebrew is a declarative statement about God ('He who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water'), not a question. The Chinese renders it as two rhetorical questions ('Can the rock become a pool? Can the flint become a spring?'), which changes the subject from God's action to a hypothetical capability of the rock, altering the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'פִּתַּחְתָּ לְמוֹסֵרָי' means 'you have loosened my bonds/fetters' (מוֹסֵרָי = my bonds), but the Chinese renders it as '你已經解開了我的帶子' ('you have untied my belt/straps'), which changes the meaning from bonds/fetters to a belt/strap.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מֵבִין פְּתָיִים' means 'gives understanding to the simple' (i.e., the naive/inexperienced). The Chinese '使人明白愚昧人' reads as 'makes people understand the foolish person' (i.e., understanding the fool as an object), which reverses the object. The correct sense is that the entrance of God's words gives understanding to the simple (the naive), not that it makes one understand fools.

omission: The Hebrew 'קִדַּמְתִּי בַנֶּשֶׁף' means 'I anticipated/prevented the twilight' (i.e., I rose before dawn), but the Chinese '我夜間起來' (I rose at night) omits the specific sense of 'anticipating/preventing' and the precise time 'twilight/evening' (נֶשֶׁף), replacing it with a general 'night'.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וָאֲשַׁוֵּעָה' means 'and I cried out/pleaded' (from שׁוע, to cry for help), but the Chinese '為你話語焦渴' (I thirst for your words) changes the action from crying out to thirsting, which is not in the Hebrew.; omission: The Hebrew 'יִחָֽלְתִּי' means 'I hoped/waited' (from יחל), but the Chinese omits this verb entirely, leaving only the thirst metaphor.
name_swap: The Hebrew place name מֶשֶׁךְ (Meshech) is rendered as '瑪士撒克' (Methuselah), which is a different name. The correct transliteration should be '米設' or '瑪設'.
addition: The Chinese adds '象牙' (ivory) which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew 'לְשִׁנֵּיהֶם' means 'to their teeth', not 'ivory'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew verb יַחֵל (from יָחַל) means 'wait for' or 'hope in', not 'call out/cry out' (קָרָא or זָעַק). The Chinese '呼求' (call out/cry out) changes the meaning from waiting/hoping to vocal petition.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְעֵדֹתִ֥י ז֗וֹ' means 'and my testimonies/statutes' (referring to God's decrees), but the Chinese renders it as '我的會眾' ('my congregation/assembly'), which is a different concept not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֹתוֹת וּמֹפְתִים' means 'signs and wonders' (two distinct terms), but the Chinese renders both as '神蹟和神蹟' (miracles and miracles), losing the distinction between 'signs' and 'wonders'.
name_swap: The Hebrew name סִיחוֹן (Sihon) is rendered as 希宏, which is an incorrect transliteration; the standard Chinese rendering is 西宏.

addition: The Chinese adds '願我的頭不再有喜樂' (may my head no longer have joy), which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has an oath formula 'if I do not remember you, if I do not raise Jerusalem above my chief joy' (implicitly, 'may my tongue stick to my palate'), but the Chinese adds a new clause about the head losing joy that has no basis in the Hebrew text.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'תַּכְלִית שִׂנְאָה שְׂנֵאתִים' means 'I hate them with perfect hatred' (or 'I hate them with utmost hatred'), where 'תַּכְלִית' is an adverb/adjective meaning 'complete/utmost' modifying 'שִׂנְאָה' (hatred), and 'שְׂנֵאתִים' is the verb 'I hate them'. The Chinese rendering '恨惡的終結就是我所恨惡的' ('the end of hatred is what I hate') misinterprets 'תַּכְלִית' as 'end/termination' and changes the subject/object relationship, making it say something different from the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'חִנָּם מְזֹרָה הָרָשֶׁת' means 'in vain is the net spread' (i.e., the net is spread in vain), referring to a net spread without cause. The Chinese renders '窮人所撒的網' ('the net spread by the poor'), introducing '窮人' (poor) which is not in the Hebrew. The subject is the net, not a person, and there is no mention of 'poor' or 'poor people' in the verse.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מְשׁוּבַת פְּתָיִם' means 'the turning away of the naive/simple ones' (פְּתָיִם = naive/simple ones, not '愚昧人' which is more like 'fools'), and 'וְשַׁלְוַת כְּסִילִים' means 'the ease/security of fools' (כְּסִילִים = fools). The Chinese renders the first clause as '愚昧人的背道而馳者' (those who turn away from the foolish), which misidentifies the subject: the Hebrew says the turning away of the naive kills them, not that those who turn away from the foolish die. The second clause '繁榮必使愚人滅亡' (prosperity will cause fools to perish) is acceptable, but the first clause is a mistranslation that changes who is doing what to whom.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'וַיֹּרֵנִי' means 'and he taught me' (from ירה, hiphil, 'to teach/instruct'), not 'he shouted to me' (歡呼). The Chinese rendering changes the action from teaching to shouting.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֹרֵתִיךָ' means 'I have taught/instructed you', not 'I gave birth to you' (which would be 'יְלִדְתִּיךָ'). The Chinese '我生了你' changes the meaning from teaching to begetting.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בִּי שָׂרִים יָשֹׂרוּ' means 'princes rule over me' or 'rulers rule by me' (the preposition בִּי can mean 'by me' or 'over me'), but the Chinese renders it as '官長因我歡欣' ('officials rejoice because of me'), which changes the meaning from ruling to rejoicing. The verb יָשֹׂרוּ is from the root שׂרר (to rule), not from a root meaning 'rejoice'.

addition: The Chinese adds '我必領你前行' (I will lead you forward), but the Hebrew first-person verb 'אֲהַלֵּךְ' means 'I walk' (first person singular), not 'I will lead you'. This changes the subject and action: the speaker walks, not leads.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יָסֻר הֵנָּה' means 'let him turn aside here' (an invitation/call), not '會轉離責備呢' (would turn away from reproof). The Chinese adds '責備' (reproof) which is not in the Hebrew, and changes the sense from an invitation to a rhetorical question about turning away.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'וְשֹׂנֵא תֹקְעִים בּוֹטֵחַ' is rendered as '而恨惡吹角者卻倚靠虛假' (but the one who hates those who strike hands trusts in falsehood). The Hebrew 'תֹקְעִים' means 'those who strike hands' (as in a pledge/guarantee), not '吹角者' (trumpeters). The Chinese mistranslates 'תֹקְעִים' as '吹角者' (horn-blower), which changes the meaning. The correct sense is 'one who hates those who pledge/guarantee (by striking hands) trusts [in them]' or similar, not 'hates trumpeters'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'טוֹב יָפִיק רָצוֹן מֵיְהוָה' means 'A good man obtains favor from the LORD' (or 'Good [man] obtains favor from the LORD'), but the Chinese renders it as '耶和華所喜悅的' ('what the LORD delights in'), shifting the subject from the good man to the LORD's favor. Additionally, 'וְאִישׁ מְזִמּוֹת יַרְשִׁיעַ' means 'but a man of wicked devices He (the LORD) condemns' (or 'a man of schemes He condemns'), but the Chinese says '比圖謀詭計的人更為正直' ('is more upright than a man of schemes'), which changes the meaning: the Hebrew contrasts the good man's favor with the wicked man's condemnation, not compares uprightness. The verb 'יַרְשִׁיעַ' (condemn/declare wicked) is mistranslated as a comparative adjective, and the subject/object relationship is altered.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְכֹסֶה קָלוֹן עָרוּם' means 'but a prudent man covers shame' (or 'one who covers shame is prudent'), i.e., the wise person conceals dishonor. The Chinese renders it as '而他赤裸的羞辱卻被遮蓋' ('but his naked shame is covered'), which reverses the subject and object: it makes the shame the subject being covered, rather than the prudent person covering shame. This introduces a non-existent name and drops the meaning 'beyond the Jordan.'

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'כָל סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ' refers to 'every boot of the booted warrior in the tumult' (i.e., the noise of battle), not '一切爭戰必因地震而起' ('all wars will arise because of earthquakes'). The Chinese adds the concept of earthquakes ('地震') and changes the meaning from the noise/tumult of battle to a cause of war, which is not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'שָׂרַי יַחְדָּו מְלָכִים' means 'are not princes together kings?' i.e., 'Are not princes kings together?' The Chinese '官長和王一同嗎' renders '官長' (officials) for 'שָׂרַי' (princes) and '王' (king) for 'מְלָכִים' (kings, plural), changing the plural 'kings' to singular 'king' and altering the sense of the rhetorical question. The Hebrew asks whether princes are also kings together, not whether officials and a king are together.

mistranslation: The Hebrew lists four place names: כַּרְכְּמִישׁ (Carchemish), כַּלְנוֹ (Calno), אַרְפַּד (Arpad), חֲמָת (Hamath), דַּמֶּשֶׂק (Damascus), שֹׁמְרוֹן (Samaria). The Chinese renders '迦勒基米士' (Carchemish) and '迦勒拿' (Calno) correctly, but '亞弗大城' is not Arpad — Arpad is a city in Syria, not 'Aphek' (亞弗). The Chinese has substituted a different place name (Aphek) for Arpad, which is a name swap.; omission: The Hebrew structure is a rhetorical question: 'Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?' The Chinese renders it as a single question '豈不都是如此嗎？' (Are they not all like this?), which collapses the three parallel rhetorical questions into one, omitting the specific comparisons (Calno vs Carchemish, Hamath vs Arpad, Samaria vs Damascus) and the repeated negation 'if not' (אִם לֹא). The reader loses the explicit parallel structure and the specific pairings.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מַעְבָּרָה' (ma'abarah) means 'ford' or 'passing place', not '渡口' (ferry crossing) — but more importantly, the clause 'גֶּבַע מָלוֹן לָנוּ' is misread: 'גֶּבַע' (Geba) is a place name, and 'מָלוֹן' (malon) means 'lodging place' or 'inn', so the phrase means 'Geba is our lodging place' (i.e., we will lodge at Geba). The Chinese renders it as '從基比亞到客店是我們的' ('from Geba to the inn is ours'), which changes the meaning: it inserts '從...到...' (from...to...) and makes the inn a separate destination, whereas the Hebrew says Geba itself is the lodging. This alters the geographical claim.; name_swap: The Hebrew 'גִּבְעַת שָׁאוּל' (Gib'at Sha'ul) means 'the hill of Saul' (Gibeah of Saul), a proper place name. The issue is that the Chinese adds '從基比亞到客店是我們的' which misconstrues the construct chain 'גֶּבַע מָלוֹן לָנוּ' as a movement from Geba to an inn, whereas the Hebrew states Geba is our lodging. mistranslation: Hebrew 'הֶמְיַת נְבָלֶיךָ' means 'the sound of your harps' (or 'the noise of your stringed instruments'), but Chinese renders it as '你琴瑟的聲音' which is correct in meaning. The issue is that the Hebrew has 'הוּרַד שְׁאוֹל' = 'brought down to Sheol' (passive), but Chinese '都下到陰間' = 'all go down to Sheol' (active). This changes the subject/voice: in Hebrew, the pride and sound are brought down (by God), whereas Chinese implies they go down by themselves. This is a tense/voice change that affects who is doing what.

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'עַד אֶגְלַיִם' (until Eglaim) and 'וּבְאֵר אֵילִים' (and Beer-elim), but the Chinese renders '以革倫' (Ekron) for Eglaim and '以琳井' (Elim well) for Beer-elim. Eglaim is a place name distinct from Ekron (עֶקְרוֹן), and Beer-elim is a specific location, not the same as Elim (אֵילִם). This swaps/drops the proper names, changing the geography.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'לֹא כֵן בַּדָּיו' (lo ken badav) is rendered as '都並非如此獨自' (all not so alone), which is unclear and likely mistranslates 'בַּדָּיו' (his boasts/empty talk). The Hebrew means 'not so his boasts' or 'his boasts are not so' — i.e., his boasting is not justified. The Chinese adds '獨自' (alone) which has no basis in the Hebrew and changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'גֶּפֶן שִׂבְמָה' means 'vine of Sibmah' (a place name), but the Chinese renders it as '示巴門的葡萄樹' ('vine of Shebam/Sheba gate'), swapping the place name Sibmah for a different name.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְרֻדַּף' is a passive verb ('and he/it is chased/driven'), but the Chinese renders it as '被驅趕' (passive, correct). This changes the meaning: the Hebrew refers to wind, not spirit. This is a mistranslation of a common noun.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'וּכְגַלְגַּל לִפְנֵי סוּפָה' means 'and like a wheel (or whirling dust) before a storm-wind' — the Chinese '又如轎輪在曠野的風暴面前' adds '曠野的' (of the wilderness) which is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has no word for 'wilderness' here; it is an addition that changes the imagery.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'יְאֹרֵי מָצוֹר' means 'the canals/streams of Egypt' (or 'of the siege'), not '城邑的溪' (streams of the city). addition: The Chinese adds '成了其國度的城樓角塔和杖' (became the corner tower and staff of its kingdom), which has no basis in the Hebrew. The Hebrew phrase 'פִּנַּ֥ת שְׁבָטֶ֖יהָ' means 'the cornerstone of her tribes' (i.e., the leaders of Egypt's tribes), not 'corner tower and staff of the kingdom.' The addition of '杖' (staff/rod) is not in the Hebrew, and the rendering misrepresents the meaning of 'פִּנַּת' as 'corner tower' rather than 'cornerstone' or 'chief.'

name_swap: The Hebrew 'בֶן אָמוֹץ' means 'son of Amoz', but the Chinese renders it as '亞摩斯城' ('the city of Amoz'), adding '城' (city) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning from a person's patronymic to a place name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תָּעָה לְבָבִי' means 'my heart is troubled/roams' (from תָּעָה, to wander/err), not '我的心驚恐' (my heart is terrified). The second clause 'פַּלָּצוּת בִּעֲתָתְנִי' means 'terror has frightened me' (פַּלָּצוּת = trembling/terror, בִּעֲתַתְנִי = it terrified me), but the Chinese renders it as '夜間的情慾使我驚恐' (nightly lust frightens me), which misidentifies the subject: 'פַּלָּצוּת' is 'terror', not '情慾' (lust/desire). The final clause 'שָׂם לִי לַחֲרָדָה' means 'he has set it for me for trembling' (i.e., made it a cause of trembling), but the Chinese omits this entirely, replacing it with a repetition of the fear idea. The translation changes the meaning: the Hebrew describes terror overwhelming the speaker and turning their cherished twilight into dread, not merely 'nightly lust causing fear'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אַרְיֵה' (aryeh) is a proper name 'Ariel' (or 'Arieh'), not the common noun 'lion' (獅子).
