This alters who is doing what.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'אֲרֻבּוֹת' means 'windows/floodgates' (of heaven), not '煙囪' (chimney). The Chinese adds a concept (chimney) not present in the Hebrew and changes the meaning of the verse's claim about the windows of heaven being opened.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הֵשַׁח יֹשְׁבֵי מָרוֹם' means 'He has brought low the inhabitants of the height' (i.e., God humbles the proud), but the Chinese renders it as '高處的居民使這高傲的城邑敗壞' ('the inhabitants of the height corrupt this proud city'), reversing the subject and object: in Hebrew, the lofty inhabitants are the object of God's action, not the agents causing the city's ruin. This changes who is doing what to whom.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יָסַפְתָּ לַגּוֹי... נִכְבָּדְתָּ' means 'You have added to the nation, O LORD, you have added to the nation; you are glorified' (i.e., the LORD is glorified/exalted), but the Chinese renders '你已將名聲傳於民族' ('you have spread your fame among the nations') and '你已將名聲傳於尊貴的民族' ('you have spread your fame among the honored nation'), which changes the subject/object: the Hebrew says the LORD is glorified (passive/reflexive sense of נִכְבָּדְתָּ), not that he spreads his fame. This alters the meaning of the verse.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'רִחַקְתָּ כָּל קַצְוֵי אָרֶץ' means 'you have removed/put far away all the ends of the earth' (i.e., you have driven them far), but the Chinese '你使一切地的極限都退後' ('you caused all the limits of the earth to retreat') is a close rendering, though '退後' (retreat) may imply the ends themselves move back, whereas the Hebrew has the LORD as agent removing them; this is acceptable. The main issue is the first clause.

addition: The Chinese adds '一剎那也不使乾渴' (not letting her thirst for a moment), which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew 'אַשְׁקֶנָּה' means 'I will water her' (i.e., give her drink), but the Chinese rendering adds the negative concept of 'not letting her be thirsty' and the time phrase '一剎那' (a moment), which is an addition not in the source.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'מִשִּׁבֹּלֶת הַנָּהָר' means 'from the stream/current of the River (Euphrates)', not 'from the ear of wheat of the great river'. The word 'שִׁבֹּלֶת' here is 'stream/current' (as in the flowing of a river), not 'ear of grain'. The Chinese '大河的耳麥' (ear of wheat of the great river) is a mistranslation of this term.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'הֲלוּמֵי יָיִן' means 'stricken/smitten with wine' (i.e., drunkards), not '沉醉於酒類的母鹿' ('a doe drunk with wine'). The word '母鹿' (doe) has no basis in the Hebrew; 'הֲלוּמֵי' is a plural participle of 'stricken' referring to people, not an animal.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְכֻפַּר בְּרִיתְכֶם אֶת מָוֶת' means 'your covenant with death will be annulled/covered' (i.e., the covenant will be atoned for/covered over, nullified). The Chinese '你們的約必蒙遮蓋' says 'your covenant will be covered' but omits the object 'death' (אֶת מָוֶת), so the reader misses that the covenant is specifically with death. This is a substantive omission of a key element.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְחָזוּתְכֶם אֶת שְׁאוֹל לֹא תָקוּם' means 'and your vision with Sheol will not stand' (i.e., your agreement with Sheol will not stand). The Chinese '你們的異象必不興起陰間' reverses the relationship: it says 'your vision will not raise up Sheol,' which changes who is doing what to whom. The Hebrew has the vision (with Sheol) not standing, not the vision causing Sheol not to rise.
name_swap: The Hebrew has 'אֲרִיאֵל' (Ariel), but the Chinese adds '雅各' (Jacob) after it, which is not present in the Hebrew text. This is an addition of a name not in the source.

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה קְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל' = 'the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel'. The Chinese renders '主耶和華神以色列' which drops 'Holy One' (קְדוֹשׁ) and misplaces 'Israel' as if it were part of the divine name, rather than 'the Holy One of Israel'.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְּשׁוּבָה וָנַחַת' means 'in returning and rest' (i.e., by turning back and being quiet), but the Chinese '歸回者與安息中' adds '者' (one who returns) and renders it as 'in the returning ones and rest', changing the sense from an action/condition to a person.

mistranslation: The Hebrew subject is second-person plural ('you said'), but the Chinese renders it as third-person feminine plural ('她們卻說'). This changes who is speaking.; number_person_tense: The Hebrew 'נָנוּס' (we will flee) is first-person plural, but the Chinese renders it as second-person plural ('你們必騎馬逃竄'), changing the subject from 'we' to 'you'.; number_person_tense: The Hebrew 'נִרְכָּב' (we will ride) is first-person plural, but the Chinese renders it as second-person plural ('你們必騎輕騎的馬'), again changing the subject.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תִּזְרֵם כְּמוֹ דָוָה צֵא תֹּאמַר לוֹ' means 'you will throw them away like a menstruous cloth; you will say to it,

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'the eyes of those who see will not look, and the ears of those who hear will listen' (or 'will be attentive'). The Chinese renders the second clause as '耳朵也必聽不見' (ears will not hear), which reverses the meaning: the Hebrew has the ears listening/being attentive, not failing to hear. This changes the claim of the verse.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּלְכִילַ֕י לֹ֥א יֵֽאָמֵ֖ר שֽׁוֹעַ' means 'and to the miserly/scoundrel it will not be said noble/generous' (i.e., the miserly will not be called noble). The Chinese renders '也不再論惡人說哀號' which says 'nor will they speak of the wicked as wailing/lamenting' — this changes the meaning: 'כִילַי' (miserly/scoundrel) is mistranslated as '惡人' (wicked), and 'שׁוֹעַ' (noble/generous) is mistranslated as '哀號' (wailing/lamentation). The verse's claim is altered: the Hebrew says the miserly will not be called noble, but the Chinese says the wicked will not be spoken of as wailing.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אִשָּׁה רְעוּתָהּ לֹא פָקָדוּ' means 'no one misses her companion' (i.e., none of them lacks its mate), not 'no one sorrowful is forgotten.' The Chinese renders 'אִשָּׁה' as '愁苦' (sorrowful) and 'פָקָדוּ' as '被遺忘' (forgotten), which changes the meaning. The verse is about none of the creatures lacking its companion, not about sorrow or forgetting.
mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'from Lachish' (מִלָּכִישׁ), not 'from the gate of Lachish' (從拉吉城門). The word 'gate' (שַׁעַר) is not present in the Hebrew text.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַסֹּפֵר' means 'the scribe' (sofer), but the Chinese renders it as '數目示巴拿' which appears to combine 'the scribe' with the name 'Shebna' (示巴拿) in a way that misidentifies the title. The Hebrew has 'וְשֶׁבְנָא הַסֹּפֵר' = 'and Shebna the scribe', but the Chinese '和數目示巴拿' seems to render 'הַסֹּפֵר' as '數目' (number/count) attached to the name, which is a mistranslation of the title 'scribe'.
mistranslation: 示巴拿這數目 is a mistranslation of וְשֶׁבְנָ֨א הַסּוֹפֵ֜ר (Shebna the scribe/secretary); '數目' (number/count) is not a rendering of 'סוֹפֵר' (scribe). This changes the meaning of the title.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'Shebna the scribe' (שֶׁבְנָא הַסּוֹפֵר), but the Chinese renders '數目示巴拿' which appears to be a mistranslation of 'the scribe' (הַסּוֹפֵר) as '數目' (number/count) instead of '書記' or '文士'. This changes the meaning of the title.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בֶן אָמוֹץ' means 'son of Amoz' (a personal name), but the Chinese renders '亞摩斯城的兒子' meaning 'son of the city of Amoz', adding '城' (city) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the proper name into a place name.

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'the king of the city of Sepharvaim' (מֶלֶךְ לָעִיר סְפַרְוָיִם), but the Chinese renders it as '西法瓦音城的王' which is correct. However, the Hebrew 'הֵנַע וְעִוָּה' refers to the gods Henna and Ivvah (or the cities Henna and Ivvah), but the Chinese translates as '希拿和以瓦在哪裡？' which is acceptable. The issue is that the Hebrew lists 'the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim' — the Chinese says '亞弗大城' for 'Arpad' which is a name swap: 'Arpad' (אַרְפָּד) is rendered as '亞弗大' instead of '亞珥拔' or similar. This changes the place name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'Isaiah son of Amoz' (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ בֶן אָמוֹץ), but the Chinese renders it as '以賽亞兒子亞摩斯城' which reads 'Isaiah son of Amoz city' — the word '城' (city) is an addition not in the Hebrew, and the construct chain is misparsed, making it appear that Amoz is a city rather than a person. This changes the identity of the sender.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'קַרְתִּי' (I dug) is rendered as '呼求' (I called out/cried out), which changes the meaning from digging wells to calling out.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְשַׂמְתִּ֨י חַחִ֜י בְּאַפֶּ֗ךָ' means 'I will put my hook in your nose' (חַח = hook/ring, אַף = nose). Chinese renders '臂環' (arm ring) and '氣' (breath/anger), which misidentifies both the object (hook vs. arm ring) and the body part (nose vs. breath/anger), changing the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יְשַׁעְיָהוּ בֶן אָמוֹץ' means 'Isaiah son of Amoz' (a personal name, Amoz). The Chinese renders it as '以賽亞兒子亞摩斯城' which reads 'Isaiah son of Amoz city' — adding '城' (city) after '亞摩斯' (Amoz), making it appear that Amoz is a city rather than a personal name. This is an addition that changes the proper name's referent.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'כְּסוּס עָגוּר' means 'like a swallow/crane' (a bird), but Chinese renders '像被圍困的燕子' adding '被圍困的' (besieged/trapped) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew has no word for 'besieged'.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'אֲצַפְצֵף' means 'I chirp/twitter' (a sound), but Chinese '我哀鳴' adds '哀' (mournful/lamenting) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew verb simply means to chirp.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'עָשְׁקָה לִּי עָרְבֵנִי' means 'oppression is upon me; be my surety/pledge for me' (imperative 'עָרְבֵנִי' = 'be my guarantor'), but Chinese '受壓迫者求你為我辯護' renders 'עָרְבֵנִי' as '為我辯護' (defend me), which changes the meaning from 'be my pledge/guarantor' to 'defend/vindicate me'; also 'עָשְׁקָה' is a noun 'oppression' not '受壓迫者' (oppressed person).

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל הַשְּׁחִין' means 'on the boil/sore' (the skin inflammation), but the Chinese renders it as '放在無花果樹的瘡瘍上' ('on the fig tree's sore'), incorrectly attributing the sore to the fig tree rather than to the person (Hezekiah). This changes the meaning of the verse.

addition: The Chinese adds '差遣使者' (sent messengers), but the Hebrew only says 'sent letters and a gift' (סְפָרִים וּמִנְחָה) — the word '使者' (messengers) is not in the Hebrew text.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וַיִּשְׁמַע כִּי חָלָה וַיֶּחֱזָק' means 'he heard that he had been sick and had recovered' — the Chinese renders '就為他痊愈而祝賀' (congratulated him on his recovery), which adds the concept of congratulation not present in the Hebrew; the Hebrew only states that he heard of the illness and recovery.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַנּוֹתֵן רוֹזְנִים לְאָיִן' means 'who makes rulers as nothing' (i.e., reduces rulers to nothing), but the Chinese renders 'רוֹזְנִים' (rulers/princes) as '光' (light), which is not in the Hebrew. The phrase 'לְאָיִן' (to nothing) is rendered as '黑暗' (darkness), which is an addition and changes the meaning. The second clause 'שֹׁפְטֵי אֶרֶץ כַּתֹּהוּ עָשָׂה' (he makes judges of the earth like chaos/formlessness) is partially correct, but the first clause is mistranslated.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'הָפֵ֤חַ בַּֽחוּרִים֙ כֻּלָּ֔ם' means 'all of them are a snare in pits' (or 'trapped in holes'), referring to people being ensnared/hidden in holes. name_swap: The Hebrew 'בִּֽישִׁמ֖וֹן' means 'in the desert/wasteland' (from יְשִׁימוֹן), not '耶示崙' (Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel). The Chinese renders it as a proper name '耶示崙', which is a mistranslation of the common noun 'wasteland'.
mistranslation: בְּחִירִי ('my chosen one') is singular, but the Chinese renders it as '我所揀選的百姓' ('my chosen people'), changing singular to plural and adding 'people'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּעָצְמַת חֲבָרַיִךְ' means 'in the strength of your spells/incantations' (חֲבָרִים = spells, charms, or incantations), not '何伯的力量' (the power of Hebo, a river god). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְלִפְנֵי יוֹם וְלֹא שְׁמַעְתָּם' means 'and before this day you had not heard of them' (referring to the things created). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יֵחָל' (from חלל, 'be profaned/defiled') is rendered as '歸於虛無' (return to nothingness/void), which changes the meaning. The Hebrew says 'how can it be profaned?' not 'how can it become nothing?'

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִי יָנוּד לָךְ' means 'who will shake [the head] for you' (i.e., lament/mourn for you), not 'who can comfort you' (which would be 'מִי יְנַחֵם'). mistranslation: Hebrew 'זְרוֹעַ קָדְשׁוֹ' means 'His holy arm' (קָדְשׁוֹ = His holiness/holy), not '祂聖所的臂膀' (the arm of His sanctuary). The Chinese adds '聖所' (sanctuary) which is not in the Hebrew; 'קָדְשׁוֹ' is an adjective 'holy' modifying 'arm', not a noun 'sanctuary'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּשְׂמֹ֖אול' means 'and left' (side), but the Chinese renders it as '左手' (left hand). While 'left hand' can idiomatically mean 'left side' in Chinese, the Hebrew word is specifically 'left' (side), not 'hand'. This is a minor semantic shift but could mislead a reader into thinking the text says 'left hand' rather than 'left side'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרִים כִּי תִמָּאֵס' means 'and a wife of youth when she is rejected' (i.e., a young wife who is rejected/despised), but the Chinese renders it as '被幼年妻子棄絕的' which reverses the subject/object: it says the man is rejected by his young wife, whereas the Hebrew says the young wife is rejected (by her husband). This changes who is doing what to whom.

number_person_tense: The Hebrew has second-person feminine singular verbs throughout (תִּכּוֹנָנִי, תִירָאִי, תִקְרַב) addressed to the city/person as 'you'. The Chinese shifts to first person '我' in '你堅立我' and '使我遠離', and then to second person '你' in '你必不懼怕' and '挨近你', mixing persons. The Hebrew consistently addresses 'you' (feminine) as the subject of being established, and the subject of fearing and the approaching destruction is 'you' as well. The Chinese rendering changes who is being established and who is being protected, and the final '挨近你' correctly uses 'you' but the earlier '我' is a person shift not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'גּוֹר יָגוּר' (surely sojourn/dwell) is rendered as '寄居的必被剪除' (sojourner will be cut off), which adds '被剪除' (cut off) not present in the Hebrew. This changes the meaning.; omission: The phrase 'אֶפֶס מֵאוֹתִי' (none from me / nothing of mine) is rendered as '無有從你中間' (none from among you), which shifts the possessive from 'my' (אוֹתִי) to 'you' (你), altering the meaning. The Hebrew says 'none of mine' (i.e., no one of my people), not 'from your midst'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נוב שְׂפָתָיִם' (nuv sefatayim) is a construct phrase meaning 'fruit of the lips' (i.e., praise/confession), but the Chinese renders it as '創造果子的嘴唇' ('creating the lips of fruit'), which reverses the construct relationship and adds '創造' (creating) that is not in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has no verb 'create' here; it is a noun phrase. This changes the meaning from 'fruit of the lips' to 'creating the lips of fruit'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְהַזּוּרֶה' means 'and the one who crushes/smashes' (from זוּר, to crush), not 'the one who tramples' (which would be רָמַס or דָּרַךְ). The Chinese '毒蛇必被壓碎' reverses the subject/object: in Hebrew the viper is the subject that emerges, not the object that is crushed.

omission: The Hebrew 'כִּי יָבוֹא כַנָּהָר צָר רוּחַ יְהוָה נֹסְסָה בוֹ' means 'for the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him' (or similar: 'the adversary comes like a river, the Spirit of the LORD raises a banner against him'). mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֶל אֲרֻבֹּתֵיהֶם' means 'to their windows/lofts' (i.e., their dovecotes or openings), not 'to chimneys' (煙囪). The Chinese adds '煙囪' (chimney) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the image.

mistranslation: The Hebrew has two parallel clauses: 'for you shall be called Hephzibah' (כִּי לָךְ יִקָּרֵא חֶפְצִי בָהּ) and 'and your land Beulah' (וּלְאַרְצֵךְ בְּעוּלָה). mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'כְּדֹרֵךְ בְּגַת' means 'like one who treads in the winepress' (or 'like a treader of the winepress'), not 'like those who tread in the city of Gath.' The Chinese translation renders it as '迦特城' (the city of Gath), which is a mistranslation of the common noun as a place name, changing the meaning of the verse.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֵת רֹעֵי צֹאנוֹ' means 'the shepherds of his flock' (referring to Moses and the leaders of Israel), but the Chinese renders it as '羊群的' (the flock's) attached to '領上' (brought up), making it 'the one who brought up the flock from the sea' instead of 'the one who brought up the shepherds of his flock from the sea'. mistranslation: Hebrew 'לֹא אֶחֱשֶׁה' means 'I will not be silent' (from חשה, to be silent), not 'I will not have mercy/compassion' (憐憫). The Chinese rendering changes the meaning from silence to mercy.
mistranslation: Hebrew לַטֶּבַח means 'for slaughter' (as in being killed), but Chinese renders it as '祭物' (sacrificial offering), which changes the meaning from slaughter to sacrifice.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'נֹטֶה' means 'stretch out' or 'extend' (of peace like a river), not '伸手' (stretch out the hand). The object is 'peace' and 'glory', not a hand. The Chinese adds '手' (hand) which is not in the Hebrew and changes the image.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'אַחַר אחד בַּתָּוֶךְ' (literally 'after one in the midst') is obscure, but the Chinese rendering '又跟隨領袖進入中間' ('and follow the leader into the midst') adds the concept of '領袖' (leader) which is not present in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has no word for 'leader'; 'אַחַר' means 'after' and 'אֶחָד' means 'one', so the phrase likely means 'one after another in the midst' or similar, not 'follow the leader'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל הַגּוֹיִם וְעַל הַמַּמְלָכוֹת' means 'over the nations and over the kingdoms' (two distinct groups: nations and kingdoms). The Chinese '在列國和列國之上' renders both as '列國' (nations), dropping the distinction of 'kingdoms' (מַמְלָכוֹת) and repeating 'nations' instead. This changes the meaning by omitting the second category.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְהַנְּבִיאִים נִבְּאוּ בַבָּעַל' means 'the prophets prophesied by Baal' (i.e., in the name of Baal). The Chinese renders '先知卻奉主人說預言' ('the prophets prophesied in the name of the master'), where '主人' (master) is an addition not present in the Hebrew and obscures the specific reference to Baal, a proper name. This changes the meaning from prophesying by the false god Baal to a generic 'master'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְגֹרְנֵךְ מִצִּמְאָה' means 'and your threshing floor from thirst' (i.e., keep your threshing floor from thirst/drought), but the Chinese renders '也不使你的打穀場遭遇口渴' which is acceptable. However, the main issue is 'וַתֹּאמְרִי נוֹאָשׁ' — the Hebrew verb is 'you said' (2fs qal perfect), not an imperative '絕望吧' (despair!). The Chinese turns it into a command, changing the person/mood. The Hebrew means 'and you said,

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נִקֵּיתִי' is a perfect (past) form meaning 'I am innocent' or 'I have been cleansed' (declaring a state of innocence), not a future passive '我必被潔淨' ('I will be cleansed'). The Chinese renders it as future, changing the claim from a present assertion of innocence to a future cleansing.
mistranslation: Hebrew זַמֹּתִי means 'I have purposed/planned/devised' (from זמם), not 'I have done evil' (行惡事). The Chinese adds the concept of doing evil that is not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מְשֻׁבוֹתֵיהֶם' (meshuvotehem) means 'their backslidings' or 'their turnings away' (from God), not 'their backsliders' or 'their ones who turn away' (背道而馳者). The Chinese '他們的背道而馳者也增強了' adds '者' (persons) and shifts the meaning from abstract 'backslidings' to 'those who turn away', changing the subject from actions to people.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְשָׁרוֹתֶיהָ' (her branches/vine-shoots) is rendered as '歌唱之處' (place of singing), which is a different meaning; the Hebrew word is from 'שׂר' (branch), not 'שיר' (song).

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שָׁמְנ֣וּ עָשְׁת֗וּ' means 'they have grown fat, they have become sleek' (referring to the wicked), but the Chinese renders '我們肥胖' ('we are fat'), changing the subject from 'they' to 'we' and altering the meaning.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'כִּרְת֣וּ עֵצָ֔ה' means 'cut down trees' (for siege works), but Chinese renders '毀壞那謀略' ('destroy that counsel/strategy'), which changes the meaning from physical action to abstract counsel.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לָמָּה זֶּה לִי לְבוֹנָה מִשְּׁבָא תָבוֹא וְקָנֶה הַטּוֹב מֵאֶרֶץ מֶרְחָק' is a rhetorical question: 'Why does frankincense come to me from Sheba, and sweet cane from a far country?' The Chinese renders it as '為何示巴人帶來的乳香...' ('Why does the Shebaites bring frankincense...'), adding '示巴人' (Shebaites) as the subject of 'bring' (帶來), whereas the Hebrew has no explicit human agent — the frankincense itself 'comes' (תָבוֹא). This changes the grammatical subject and adds an agent not present in the Hebrew.; omission: The Hebrew 'עֹלוֹתֵיכֶם לֹא לְרָצוֹן וְזִבְחֵיכֶם לֹא עָרְבוּ לִי' is a separate declarative statement: 'Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not pleasing to me.' The Chinese renders it as a continuation of the rhetorical question ('你們的燔祭不蒙悅納，你們的祭物我也不喜悅？'), turning the declarative into an interrogative, which changes the force of the verse. The Hebrew has no interrogative particle here; the question is only in the first clause.
addition: The Chinese adds '就必蒙福' (then you will be blessed), which is not present in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew only states the conditional clauses without an explicit result clause.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְקַטֵּר לַבָּעַל' means 'and burn incense to Baal' (i.e., to the god Baal), but the Chinese renders it as '向主人獻香' ('offer incense to the master'), which changes the proper name 'Baal' to a generic 'master' (主人). This is a name swap that alters the meaning.
name_swap: The Hebrew 'בָּמוֹת הַתֹּפֶת' (high places of Topheth) is rendered as '他泊的高處' (high places of Tabor), substituting the place name Topheth with Tabor, which is a different location.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'מֵי רֹאשׁ' (waters of poison/bitter water) is rendered as '那頭的水' (the water of that head), which is a mistranslation. 'רֹאשׁ' here means 'poison' or 'bitter', not 'head'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְתִשֶּׂנָה עָלֵינוּ נֶהִי' means 'and they (fem.) lift up a lament over us' (i.e., raise a wailing over us), not 'attack us' (攻擊我們). The verb נָשָׂא with נֶהִי means 'to lift up a lamentation', not 'to attack'. The Chinese '攻擊我們' introduces a hostile military action not present in the Hebrew, changing the meaning.

mistranslation: Hebrew נִבְעֲרוּ (from בער, 'to be stupid/brutish') means 'have become stupid/brutish', not 'have been destroyed/removed' (被除滅). The Chinese rendering changes the meaning of the clause.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לַבָּעַל' (to Baal) is rendered as '向主人' (to the master/lord), which changes the proper name Baal into a common noun. This is a name swap that alters the meaning.
mistranslation: The Hebrew has 'בַּבָּעַל' (by Baal), but the Chinese renders it as '主人' (master/lord), which loses the proper name Baal and changes the referent.

omission: The Hebrew 'וְדָמֹעַ תִּדְמַע' (weeping and weeping / surely weep) is rendered as '眼要流淚' (eyes will shed tears), which omits the explicit doubling of weeping (the infinitive absolute + finite verb) and the separate mention of weeping as an action distinct from tears. The Chinese loses the emphatic 'surely weep' and the parallel structure of 'weep' and 'tears'.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נַפְשִׁי' (my soul) is rendered as '性命' (life), which is acceptable, but the clause 'תִּבְכֶּה נַפְשִׁי' (my soul shall weep) is rendered as '性命悲哀' (life is sorrowful), shifting the verb from 'weep' to 'be sorrowful', a change in meaning.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִפְּנֵי גֵוָה' (because of pride) is rendered as '因驕傲' (because of pride), which is correct, but the phrase 'בְּמִסְתָּרִים' (in secret places) is rendered as '在隱密處' (in a secret place), which is acceptable. This loses the specific imagery of the eye running down with tears.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כִּי נִשְׁבָּה עֵדֶר יְהוָה' (for the flock of the LORD is taken captive) is rendered as '因耶和華的羊群被擄去' (because the flock of the LORD is taken captive), which is correct. However, the verb 'נִשְׁבָּה' (is taken captive) is rendered as '被擄去' (is taken away captive), which is acceptable. No issue here.

omission: The Hebrew 'שאי עיניכם וראי' means 'Lift up your eyes and see' (imperative), but the Chinese '不要讓你們的眼目轉離' means 'Do not let your eyes turn away', which reverses the command and omits the 'see' action.
mistranslation: Hebrew חָשַׂפְתִּי means 'I have uncovered/exposed', but Chinese says '遮蓋' (cover), reversing the action.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל הָאָבְנָיִם' means 'on the potter's wheels' (dual of 'אָבְנַיִם', a pair of wheels/stones used in pottery). The Chinese renders it as 'on the stone' (石頭上), which is a mistranslation—it should be 'on the wheels' or 'on the potter's wheel(s)'. This changes the specific object/place of the work.

name_swap: The Hebrew says the place will no longer be called 'the Topheth' (הַתֹּפֶת) and 'the Valley of the son of Hinnom' (גֵּיא בֶן הִנֹּם), but the Chinese renders 'the Topheth' as '他泊' (Tabor), which is a different place name (Tabor, a mountain). The correct rendering should be '陀斐特' or similar for Topheth.
name_swap: Hebrew has בְּתֹפֶת ('in Topheth'), but Chinese renders it as 他泊 ('Tabor'), which is a different place name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כִּמְקוֹם הַתֹּפֶת' means 'like the place of Topheth' (a specific location, Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom), but the Chinese renders it as '像他泊那被玷污的地方' ('like Tabor, that defiled place'), substituting 'Tabor' (תָּבוֹר) for 'Topheth' (הַתֹּפֶת). This is a name swap: 'Topheth' is a proper place name, not a common noun meaning 'defiled place'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּבָבֶ֣ל תָּב֗וֹא' means 'and you will come to Babylon' (you, Pashhur, will go to Babylon). The Chinese '巴比倫必來到' reverses the subject/object, making Babylon come to you, which changes who is doing what.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'פִּתִּיתַנִי' (from פָּתָה, 'to entice/deceive') is rendered as '使我開口' ('made me open my mouth'), which changes the meaning from 'You enticed/deceived me' to 'You caused me to speak'. This is a substantive mistranslation of the verb.; omission: The Hebrew 'וָאֶפָּת' ('and I was enticed/deceived') is rendered as '我便受感說話' ('and I was moved to speak'), which omits the core meaning of being deceived/enticed and replaces it with a different concept.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'חֲזַקְתַּנִי וַתּוּכָל' ('You have overcome me and prevailed') is rendered as '祂堅固我，我也勝過' ('He strengthened me, and I also overcame'), which reverses the subject/object: in Hebrew, YHWH overcomes the speaker, but the Chinese says the speaker overcomes. This changes who is doing what to whom.

name_swap: The Hebrew has 'פַּשְׁחוּר בֶּן מַלְכִּיָּה' (Pashhur son of Malkijah) and 'צְפַנְיָה בֶן מַעֲשֵׂיָה' (Zephaniah son of Maaseiah). The Chinese reverses the father-son relationships: it says '巴實錄兒子瑪基雅' (Pashhur's son Malkijah) and '祭司西番雅兒子瑪西雅' (priest Zephaniah's son Maaseiah), swapping the names so that the sons become fathers and vice versa.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מְתַחֲרֶה בָאָרֶז' means 'vying/competing in cedar' (i.e., striving for cedar for building), not '爭著吃雪松' ('vying to eat cedar'). The Chinese adds '吃' (eat), which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning.

So the Chinese has reversed the subject and object of the going. This is a clear mistranslation.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'רַב טַבָּחִים' (rav tabbachim) is a title meaning 'chief of the guards' or 'captain of the guard' (a proper military title), not '多屬宰殺者的' ('many belonging to slaughterers'). The Chinese rendering misinterprets the title, changing the meaning of who led the Chaldean forces.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְאֵת יֶתֶר הָאָמוֹן' means 'and the rest of the multitude/people' (הָאָמוֹן = the multitude/rabble), but Chinese renders it as '剩下的工匠' (the remaining craftsmen/artisans). 'אָמוֹן' does not mean 'craftsman' (that would be 'חָרָשׁ' or similar); it means a crowd/multitude. This changes the meaning of the verse.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'רוּחָה' (ruach) here means 'side' or 'direction' (referring to the pomegranates facing outward on each side), not '靈' (spirit). The Chinese '靈' is a mistranslation that changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בִּידֵ֖י לֹא אוּכַ֥ל קֽוּם' means 'in [whose] hands I cannot rise' (i.e., I am delivered into hands from which I cannot rise), but the Chinese '主將我交在無法站立的人手中' renders it as 'the Lord delivered me into the hands of people who cannot stand,' changing the subject of inability from the speaker to the people. mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַּת עֵינֵךְ' means 'the daughter of your eye' (i.e., your eye/pupil), not '你眼中的女兒' (the daughter in your eye). The Chinese rendering '你眼中的女兒' could be misread as a literal daughter, whereas the Hebrew idiom refers to the eye itself. This changes the meaning of the final clause.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֹיְבִ֥י כִלָּֽם' means 'my enemy has consumed/annihilated them' (the enemy is the subject of the verb, consuming the ones I raised). The Chinese renders it as '祂已盡滅其敵' ('He has completely destroyed His enemies'), reversing the subject and object: in Hebrew, the enemy destroys the nurtured ones, not God destroying the enemy. This changes who is doing what to whom.

addition: The Chinese adds '直到耶和華從天垂看' (until the LORD looks down from heaven), which has no basis in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew only states that the eye flows and does not cease for lack of relief; it does not mention the LORD looking down from heaven.

name_swap: The Hebrew place name כְּבָר (Kebar) is a river, not a city; the Chinese renders it as '基伯城' (city of Kebar), adding '城' (city) which is not in the Hebrew and misidentifies the river as a city.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'on the river Chebar' (עַל נְהַר כְּבָר), but the Chinese renders it as '基伯城的大河邊' (the great river of the city of Gibber/Keber), adding '城' (city) and '大' (great) which are not in the Hebrew, and misidentifying the river as associated with a city.

name_swap: The Hebrew text says 'עַל נְהַר כְּבָר' (on/by the river Chebar), but the Chinese renders it as '基伯城大河' (the great river of the city of Kibar), adding '城' (city) and changing 'כְּבָר' (Chebar, a river name) into a city name. This is a factual error: Chebar is a river, not a city.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שְׁנֵי עֲוֹנָם' means 'the two iniquities' (i.e., the iniquity of both houses, Judah and Israel), but the Chinese renders it as '他們二人的罪惡' ('the sins of the two of them'), which is ambiguous and could be read as 'two persons' rather than 'two iniquities' or 'the iniquity of the two (houses)'. This changes the referent from the two sins/houses to possibly two individuals.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'לְכָל רֽוּחַ' means 'to every wind' (i.e., scatter to all directions), but the Chinese renders it as '到一切靈那裏' ('to every spirit'), which changes the meaning from a physical scattering to the winds to a spiritual destination. This is a mistranslation of 'רוּחַ' (wind) as '靈' (spirit).

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְהַשְּׁלִישִׁית לְכָל רוּחַ אֱזָרֶה' means 'and the third I will scatter to every wind' — the Chinese '一切的靈我必拔刀追趕他們' renders 'רוּחַ' (wind) as '靈' (spirit), and 'אֱזָרֶה' (I will scatter) as '拔刀追趕' (draw sword and pursue), which changes the meaning. The Hebrew says the third part is scattered to every wind, not that spirits are pursued with a sword.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַצְּפִרָה' (hatzefirah) means 'the crown' or 'the diadem' (from צָפִיר, a crown/garland), not '冠冕' (crown) — actually '冠冕' is correct for 'crown'. However, 'הַמַּטֶּה' (hammatteh) means 'the rod/staff/scepter' (a branch or staff), not '杖已飛逝' (the staff has flown away). The Chinese '杖已飛逝' incorrectly renders 'צָץ' (budded/blossomed) as '飛逝' (flew away), changing the meaning. Also 'פָּרַח הַזָּדוֹן' means 'arrogance has blossomed' (פָּרַח = to blossom/flourish), which the Chinese renders as '驕傲已綻放' (arrogance has blossomed) — that is correct. The main error is the mistranslation of 'צָץ הַמַּטֶּה' as '杖已飛逝' instead of 'the rod has budded'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'הַנָּשִׁים' means 'the women', but the Chinese renders it as '妻子' (wives), which changes the meaning from a group of women to specifically wives. This is a mistranslation of the noun.

name_swap: The Hebrew place name is כְּבָר (Kebar, a river in Babylon), but the Chinese renders it as 基伯城 (city of Gibber?), adding 城 (city) and changing the name; the Hebrew says 'river Kebar' (נְהַר כְּבָר), not a city.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בִּנְהַר כְּבָר' means 'by the river Chebar' (a place name, the Chebar River), but the Chinese renders it as '大河基伯城' ('the great river, city of Kiber'), adding '城' (city) and misidentifying the river as a city. The Hebrew has no 'city' concept here.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּנוֹת בָּתִּים' (literally 'daughters of houses') is rendered as '家中的女兒們' (daughters in the house), which is a plausible reading, but the key issue is the rendering of 'לֹא בְקָרוֹב' as '必不久於人世' (will not be long in the world). The Hebrew 'לֹא בְקָרוֹב' means 'not soon' or 'not in the near future,' referring to the time of the prophecy's fulfillment, not to death. The Chinese adds the concept of death ('於人世') and changes the meaning to 'will not live long,' which is a substantive addition and mistranslation. The original says 'not soon' regarding building houses, not about the daughters' lifespan.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְהַנָּשִׂיא' means 'the prince/leader' (נָשִׂיא), not '元帥' (military commander/general). This changes the identity of the subject.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בָּעֲלָטָה' means 'in the dark' or 'at twilight' (עֲלָטָה = darkness), not '走入昏暗' (walk into darkness). The phrase 'יִשָּׂא בָּעֲלָטָה' means 'he shall carry [his belongings] in the dark' — the carrying is done in darkness, not walking into darkness. The Chinese adds '走入' (walk into) which is not in the Hebrew.; omission: The Hebrew 'בַּקִּיר יַחְתְּרוּ לְהוֹצִיא בוֹ' means 'they shall dig through the wall to bring [him] out through it' — the purpose clause 'לְהוֹצִיא בוֹ' (to bring out through it) is omitted in the Chinese, which only says '穿過牆逃離' (escape through the wall), losing the explicit purpose of bringing him out.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'פָּנָיו יְכַסֶּה' means 'he shall cover his face' (active, the prince covers his own face), but the Chinese '他必蒙住臉' is ambiguous — it could be read as passive (his face will be covered by others). The Hebrew is clearly active: the subject covers his own face.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יַעַן אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִרְאֶה לַעַיִן הוּא אֶת הָאָרֶץ' means 'because he shall not see with his eye the land' — the Chinese '因他眼不見地' (because his eyes do not see the land) is close, but the Hebrew emphasizes 'with his eye' (לַעַיִן) which is not fully captured; however this is minor and could be considered acceptable. The main issue is the earlier mistranslations.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עזרה' (help/helper) is rendered as '幫助者' (helper), which is acceptable, but 'אֲגַפָּיו' (his wings/forces) is translated as '臂' (arms), which is a mistranslation; 'אֲגַפָּיו' means 'his wings' or 'his forces/bands', not 'arms'. Also, 'אֱזָרֶה' (I will scatter) is rendered as '束縛' (bind/restrain), which is a mistranslation; the Hebrew means 'I will scatter' (to all winds), not 'bind'. The phrase 'לְכָל רוּחַ' (to every wind) is rendered as '為一切靈' (for all spirits), which changes the meaning from 'wind' to 'spirit'. The final clause 'וְחֶרֶב אָרִיק אַחֲרֵיהֶם' (and I will draw out a sword after them) is rendered as '刀劍向他們四面揮動' (swords wave around them on all sides), which adds '四面' (all sides) not in the Hebrew and changes 'draw out' to 'wave'.

addition: The Chinese adds '我必使' (I will cause) for the hail stones, but the Hebrew has no first-person subject; the clause is 'and you (fem. pl.) shall fall as stones of hail' — the subject is the stones, not God acting.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְאַתֵּנָה אַבְנֵי אֶלְגָּבִישׁ תִּפֹּלְנָה' means 'and you (fem. pl.) shall fall as stones of hail' — the addressees (the foolish plasterers) are told they will fall like hail stones. The Chinese renders this as '我必使雹石降下' (I will cause hail stones to fall), changing the subject from the addressees to God and losing the simile 'as stones of hail'.; omission: The Hebrew 'אֶל טָחֵי תָפֵל' means 'to those who plaster with whitewash' — the Chinese '對無知之物說' (speak to ignorant things) omits the specific reference to the plasterers and the whitewash, replacing it with a generic 'ignorant things' that is not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וָאֶעְדֵּךְ עֶדִי' means 'I adorned you with ornaments' (from עדי, 'ornament/adornment'), not 'I made you a lowly one' (亞低). The Chinese '亞低' appears to be a transliteration error or misreading; it should convey 'adorned you with jewelry/ornaments'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בִּבְנוֹתַיִךְ גַּבֵּךְ' means 'in your building your back' (i.e., 'when you built your back'), but the Chinese renders '在你女兒們的脊背' ('on the backs of your daughters'), misreading 'בִּבְנוֹתַיִךְ' (in your building) as 'בְּנוֹתַיִךְ' (your daughters). This changes the meaning from 'when you built your back' to 'on your daughters' backs'.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְרָמָתֵךְ עָשִׂיתִי' means 'and I made your high place' (or 'your height'), but the Chinese '我在一切街道上為你設立了拉瑪' adds '在一切街道上' ('in all streets') and renders 'רָמָתֵךְ' as the place name '拉瑪' (Ramah) rather than 'your high place/height'. This is a mistranslation and an addition of location not in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'לֹֽא זכרתי' means 'you did not remember' (2fs), but Chinese says '你忘記了' (you forgot) — acceptable. However, 'וְלֹ֤א עשיתי אֶת הַזִּמָּה' means 'I have not done the lewdness' (1cs), but Chinese says '我必不赦免你的惡行' (I will not forgive your evil deeds), which adds 'forgive' and changes the meaning from 'I have not done' to 'I will not forgive'.; addition: Chinese adds '赦免' (forgive) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew states 'I have not done the lewdness' (a denial of action), not a refusal to forgive.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְגַם אֲנִי הֵ֜א דַּרְכֵּךְ בְּרֹ֣אשׁ נָתַ֗תִּי' means 'I also have set your way upon your head' (I have brought your conduct back on you), but Chinese '我也必將你的路放在你頭上' is close, yet the following clause misrepresents the Hebrew's 'I have not done the lewdness' as 'I will not forgive your evil deeds'.
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'דָּיֵק' means 'siege wall' or 'siege tower', not '勇士' (warriors). The Chinese renders '建造勇士' (building warriors), which is a mistranslation of the term.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְשִׁנֵּי הַבָּנִים תִּקְהֶינָה' means 'and the children's teeth are set on edge' (i.e., become blunt/dull), but the Chinese renders it as '兒女的象牙就酸了' ('the children's ivory becomes sour'), which changes the meaning from teeth being affected to ivory being sour, and introduces '象牙' (ivory) not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'פֶּטֶר רָחַם' means 'that which opens the womb' (firstborn offspring), but Chinese renders '初生的肚腸' ('firstborn intestines/bowels'), which is a mistranslation of 'רָחַם' (womb) as '肚腸' (intestines).

negation: The Hebrew 'אִם אִדָּרֵשׁ לָכֶם' is an oath formula meaning 'if I am sought by you' (i.e., I will not be sought by you), but the Chinese renders it as '我必不再尋問你們' (I will no longer seek you), reversing the subject-object relationship: in Hebrew, the people seek God, not God seeking them. This changes who is doing the seeking.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'מִתַּעְרָהּ' means 'from its sheath/scabbard', not 'from a razor' (剃刀). The Chinese renders 'from its sheath' as 'from a razor', changing the object from a sword's scabbard to a razor.
mistranslation: Hebrew 'מִתַּעְרָהּ' means 'from its sheath' (scabbard), not 'from a razor' (剃刀). The Chinese renders '剃刀' (razor), which is a mistranslation of the noun 'תַּעַר' (sheath).
mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מִתַּעְרָהּ' means 'from its sheath/scabbard', but the Chinese renders it as '從剃刀出' ('from the razor'), which is a mistranslation of the noun 'תַּעַר' (sheath) as 'razor'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'אִבְחַת חָרֶב' means 'the slaughter of the sword' or 'the flashing of the sword' (a sword's edge/glint), not '刀劍的亞比加' (the 'Abiga' of the sword). 'אִבְחַת' is a noun meaning 'slaughter' or 'flash/glint', not a proper name. The Chinese adds a transliterated name '亞比加' that has no basis in the Hebrew.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'מְעֻטָּה לְטָבַח' means 'wrapped/polished for slaughter' (i.e., the sword is prepared for killing), not '作閃電中微少的祭物' ('as a small sacrifice in the lightning'). 'מְעֻטָּה' is a passive participle meaning 'wrapped' or 'polished', and 'לְטָבַח' means 'for slaughter', not 'a small sacrifice'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'טְמֵאַת הַנִּדָּה עִנּוּ בָךְ' means 'they humbled/afflicted the woman unclean through menstruation in you' (i.e., they violated the menstruous woman). The Chinese '玷污了不潔之物' ('defiled the unclean thing') misidentifies the object as an inanimate thing rather than a person (the menstruous woman), and omits the explicit subject 'they' (implied in the verb עִנּוּ) and the verb's sense of afflicting/humbling a person. This changes who is doing what to whom.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'פַּחוֹת וּסְגָנִים' means 'governors and officials' (or 'deputies and prefects'), not '百夫長和王子' (centurions and princes). The Chinese rendering swaps the social/political titles for different ones.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'בַּחוּרֵי חֶמֶד' means 'desirable young men' or 'choice young men' (i.e., young men of beauty/desire), not '一切的少年人在恩愛中' ('all the young men in love/affection'). The Chinese adds the concept of 'in love/affection' (恩愛中) which is not in the Hebrew, and '一切的' (all) is an addition not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּנֵי אַשּׁוּר' means 'sons of Assyria' (i.e., Assyrians), not '亞述人的兒子' (sons of the Assyrian people) — the Chinese adds '人' (people) which is a minor addition but not substantive. More importantly, 'פַּחוֹת וּסְגָנִים' means 'governors and officials' (or 'deputies and rulers'), not '百夫長與王子' (centurions and princes) — this is a mistranslation of both terms. 'קְרֹבִים' means 'near/close ones' (i.e., those close to them), not '親近的人' which is acceptable, but the overall rendering of the officials' titles is wrong. 'בַּחוּרֵי חֶמֶד' means 'desirable young men' (choice young men), not '少年人在恩愛中' (young men in love) — 'חֶמֶד' means 'desire/pleasantness', not '恩愛' (affection/love). The phrase 'כֻּלָּם' means 'all of them', which is preserved as '一切'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְעָדִית עֶדִי' means 'and adorned yourself with jewelry/ornaments' (the verb עָדָה with the noun עֶדִי as its object). The Chinese renders 'עֶדִי' as a place name '亞低' (a transliteration), which is a mistranslation — it is not a place name but the noun 'ornament/jewelry'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שָׂמָתְהוּ' (she placed it) has the feminine subject referring to the city (her), and the object 'it' refers to the blood. The Chinese '她被放在' (she was placed) changes the subject to the blood/city being placed, and makes it passive, altering who is doing the action. The Hebrew says the city placed the blood on a bare rock, not that she was placed there.

omission: The Hebrew 'דֹּם' (be silent/be still) is omitted; the Chinese only renders 'הֵאָנֵק' (groan/sigh) as '不要哀號' but does not convey the command to be silent.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְלֹא תַעְטֶה עַל שָׂפָם' means 'and you shall not cover your upper lip' (a mourning custom), but the Chinese renders it as '不可剃掉鬍子' (do not shave off the beard), which is a different action not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase וּמַחְמַ֣ל נַפְשְׁכֶ֑ם means 'the object of your soul's compassion/pity' (i.e., something you deeply care for), but the Chinese renders it as '性命的皮衣' ('leather garment of your life'), which is a mistranslation. The word מַחְמַל is from the root חמל (to spare/have compassion), not related to leather or clothing.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'עַל שָׂפָם לֹא תַעְטוּ' means 'you shall not cover your upper lip' (a mourning custom), but Chinese says '不可剃鬍子' (you shall not shave your beard), which changes the action from covering to shaving.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּכָל שָׁאטְךָ בְּנֶפֶשׁ' means 'with all your contempt/scorn in your soul' (i.e., with all your soul's contempt), but the Chinese renders it as '以性命歡喜' (rejoice with your life/soul), which changes the meaning from 'contempt' to 'life/soul' as the object of rejoicing. The Hebrew 'שָׁאטְךָ' (your contempt/scorn) is not represented; instead 'נֶפֶשׁ' (soul) is taken as the instrument of rejoicing, whereas in Hebrew it is the soul that harbors the contempt.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'צְבִי אֶרֶץ' means 'the glory of the land' or 'the pride of the land', not '地的母鹿' (the doe of the land). The word 'צְבִי' is a noun meaning 'glory/beauty', not 'doe' (which would be 'צְבִיָּה'). This changes the meaning of the verse.; name_swap: The Hebrew 'קְרִיָּתַיְמָה' (Kiriathaim) is rendered as '基列亞音' (Gilead-ayin?), which appears to be a conflation or misreading. The correct transliteration should be '基列亭' or '基利亞亭' (Kiriathaim). The rendering '基列亞音' introduces a different place name element ('Gilead') not present in the Hebrew.
mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'in the eleventh year' (בְּעַשְׁתֵּֽי עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָה), but the Chinese says '在十年一月' (in the tenth year, first month), which changes the year from 11 to 10.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְנָתַן עָלַיִךְ דָּיֵק' means 'he will set a siege wall against you' (דָּיֵק = siege wall/rampart), but Chinese renders '他必使勇士攻擊你' ('he will make warriors attack you'), introducing '勇士' (warriors) not in the Hebrew and changing the meaning from a siege structure to an attack by warriors.

mistranslation: Hebrew וּפְרָדִים means 'mules' (or possibly 'horses' in some contexts, but here clearly 'mules' as distinct from סוּסִים 'horses'), but Chinese renders it as '驢子' (donkeys). This is a factual difference in animal type.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'בְבִגְדֵי חֹפֶשׁ' means 'in garments of freedom/loose garments' (i.e., mantles/cloaks), not '貴重的馬毯' (precious horse blankets). The Chinese adds '貴重' (precious) and '馬毯' (horse blanket) which is not in the Hebrew; the Hebrew refers to clothing, not horse blankets.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וַהֲשִׁבֹתִי אֹתָם אֶרֶץ פַּתְרוֹס עַל אֶרֶץ מְכוּרָתָם' means 'and I will bring them back to the land of Pathros, to the land of their origin' — the Chinese reverses the direction: it says '將他們從生處之地帶回帕特羅斯' ('bring them from the land of their origin back to Pathros'), implying they are taken out of their origin land to Pathros, whereas the Hebrew says they are returned to Pathros, which is their origin land. This changes the meaning of the clause.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'הַדָּמִין יִתְעֲבֵד וּבַיְתֵהּ נְוָלִי יִשְׁתַּוֵּה' means 'shall be cut in pieces, and their houses shall be made a dunghill' (i.e., the offender and his house). The Chinese renders only '必將他扔進烈火的糞堆中' ('will throw him into the fiery dung heap'), which conflates the two punishments: it omits the dismemberment ('cut in pieces') and misplaces the 'dunghill' as a fiery place of execution rather than the destruction of the house. This changes the factual content of the decree.; omission: The Hebrew 'וּבַיְתֵהּ נְוָלִי יִשְׁתַּוֵּה' ('and his house shall be made a dunghill') is entirely omitted; the Chinese only mentions throwing the person into a fiery dung heap, losing the separate punishment on the house.

omission: The Hebrew lists four groups: חרטמיא (magicians), אשפיא (enchanters), כשדיא (Chaldeans), and גזריא (diviners). The Chinese omits 'magicians' (חרטמיא) and 'enchanters' (אשפיא), rendering only '迦勒底人、術士、巫師' (Chaldeans, sorcerers, diviners), which drops two of the four categories.

mistranslation: Hebrew עִדָּנִין (iddanin) means 'times' or 'periods' (Aramaic plural of עִדָּן, 'time'), not '青春時期' (youth/prime periods). The phrase '七個時期' (seven periods/times) is the correct rendering; '青春時期' adds a specific meaning of youth/adolescence not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says 'they commanded to leave the stump of its roots of the tree' (לְמִשְׁבַּק עִקַּר שָׁרְשׁוֹהִי דִּי אִילָנָא), i.e., the command was to leave the stump and roots of the tree. The Chinese renders it as 'they commanded to seek the one who cuts down the tree and leaves the stump and roots' (他們囑咐要尋找那砍伐樹木、留下樹樁和根的人), adding '尋找' (seek) and '那砍伐樹木...的人' (the one who cuts down the tree), which is not in the Hebrew. This changes the subject/action: the Hebrew command is about leaving the stump, not about seeking a person.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּמִחַן עֲנָיִן' means 'by showing mercy to the poor/afflicted' (with 'עֲנָיִן' = 'the poor/afflicted'), but the Chinese renders it as '在亞拿雅面前受試煉' ('tested before Ananiah'), which misidentifies 'עֲנָיִן' as a proper name '亞拿雅' and adds the concept of 'being tested' not present in the Hebrew. The correct meaning is that the king's iniquities are to be atoned for by showing mercy to the poor.; omission: The Hebrew 'מִלְכִּי יִשְׁפַּר עֲלַיִךְ' means 'let my counsel be acceptable to you' (the speaker's counsel), but the Chinese '謀士為你求告' ('the counselor prays for you') omits the first-person possessive 'my' and changes the meaning from 'my counsel' to a generic 'counselor' praying, losing the speaker's direct offer of advice.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says the queen entered the banquet house 'in response to the words of the king and his nobles' (לָקֳבֵל מִלֵּי מַלְכָּא וְרַבְרְבָנוֹהִי לְבֵית מִשְׁתְּיָא עַלַּת). The Chinese reverses the subject/object: it says 'the queen... from the banquet house came to the queen' (從筵席的家起身，來到王后面前), which misidentifies who enters and who is addressed. The Hebrew has the queen entering the banquet house and speaking to the king; the Chinese has someone coming from the banquet house to the queen, and the queen speaking. This changes who is doing what to whom.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תְּקֵל' (teqel) is transliterated as '他刻爾' (tā kè ěr), which adds an extra syllable '爾' not present in the Hebrew. The correct transliteration should be '提客勒' or similar, without the extra '爾'.

omission: The Hebrew mentions 'another horn came up' (וְאָחֳרִי דִּי סִלְקַת) and that this horn had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and its appearance was greater than its companions. The Chinese omits the explicit mention of the 'another horn' that came up, instead saying '又有一個角' (another horn) but does not clearly convey that it 'came up' (סִלְקַת). Also, the Hebrew says 'three fell before it' (נְפַלוּ מִן קֳדָמַהּ תְּלָת), which the Chinese renders as '三個角被拔去' (three horns were pulled out), changing the action from 'fell before it' to 'were pulled out'—a mistranslation of the verb and the relationship.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'יְהַעְדּוֹן' means 'they will take away/remove' (Aramaic), but Chinese renders '必被證實' ('will be confirmed'), which reverses the meaning. The verse says the dominion will be removed/destroyed, not confirmed.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל אוּבַל אוּלָי' means 'by the Ulai canal' (a waterway), not '在幼伯河的烏來城' ('in the city of Ulai on the Yubai River'). The Ulai is a river/canal, not a city, and 'עַל' means 'by/at' not 'in'. This changes the location from a canal to a city.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַּעַל הַקְּרָנַיִם' means 'the ram with two horns' (possessor of the horns), but the Chinese renders it as '有角的公羊' (horned ram), which is acceptable. However, the phrase '那主人' (that master) is an addition not in the Hebrew; 'בַּעַל' here is part of the construct 'בַּעַל הַקְּרָנַיִם' meaning 'possessor of the horns', not 'master/owner' as a separate entity. This addition changes the meaning by introducing a 'master' who runs, whereas the Hebrew subject is the ram itself.; addition: The Chinese adds '那主人' (that master) as the subject of '滿懷怒氣與能力向它跑去', but the Hebrew 'וַיָּרָץ אֵלָיו בַּחֲמַת כֹּחוֹ' has the ram as the implied subject (he ran to it in the fury of his strength). The addition of a 'master' is not in the Hebrew and changes who is running.

name_swap: The Hebrew proper name חִדָּקֶל (Hiddekel, i.e. the Tigris) is rendered as '基德爾河' (Jidé'ěr River), which is not the standard Chinese name for the Tigris (底格里斯河). This is a name swap/error that would mislead the reader.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אִישׁ חֲמֻדוֹת' means 'man of preciousness/desirability' (i.e., 'highly esteemed/treasured man'), not '貪戀的人' ('covetous person'). The Chinese rendering changes the meaning from a term of honor to a negative description.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'רוּחוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם' means 'winds of heaven' (four winds), but Chinese renders '天的四靈' ('four spirits of heaven'), changing 'winds' to 'spirits'.; mistranslation: Hebrew 'וְלֹא כְמָשְׁלוֹ אֲשֶׁר מָשָׁל' means 'not according to his dominion which he ruled' (i.e., not with the same power/dominion as before), but Chinese '也不像那曾掌權的' ('nor like the one who once ruled') shifts the subject from the kingdom's dominion to a person, altering the meaning.; addition: Chinese '而非獨自存留' ('rather than remaining alone') adds a concept not present in Hebrew 'מִלְּבַד אֵלֶּה' ('apart from these'), which simply means 'to others besides these' — the Chinese phrase introduces an idea of solitary survival not in the source.

mistranslation: The Hebrew says the southern king will go out and fight with him (the northern king), and the great multitude will be given into his hand (the southern king's hand). The Chinese says the multitude will be given into the northern king's hand, reversing the recipient.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'וְעַל חֶמְדַּת נָשִׁים' means 'the desire of women' (i.e., the object of women's desire, often understood as a reference to a deity or idol women cherish), not '妻子的寶物' (wife's treasure). The Chinese rendering narrows 'women' to 'wife' and changes 'desire' to 'treasure,' altering the meaning.

mistranslation: Hebrew בַּסִּירִים means 'with thorns' (plural of סִיר, thorn/bramble), not 'with pots' (鍋子). The Chinese '鍋子' is a mistranslation of the noun.; mistranslation: Hebrew גְּדֵרָהּ refers to 'her wall' (the wall of the woman/path), not 'your sheepfold' (羊圈). The Chinese '你的羊圈' adds 'your' and changes the referent from 'her wall' to 'your sheepfold'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עָשׂוּ לַבָּעַל' means 'they made [it] for Baal' (i.e., used the silver and gold to make idols for Baal). The Chinese renders this as '他們卻用來獻給主人' ('they used it to offer to the master'), which changes 'Baal' (a proper name of the deity) to '主人' (master/lord), losing the specific reference to Baal and altering the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'כְּבוֹדָ֖ם בְּקָל֥וֹן אָמִֽיר' means 'I will turn their glory into shame' (or 'their glory I will change into disgrace'), but the Chinese renders it as '他們的榮耀在於羞辱' ('their glory consists in shame'), which changes the meaning from a divine action of transformation to a static description. The verb 'אָמִיר' (I will change/exchange) is omitted, and the sense of future divine judgment is lost.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אַיְסִרֵם' (I will discipline/correct them) is rendered as '召集' (gather/assemble), which changes the meaning. The Hebrew verb means to discipline or chastise, not to gather.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַּגִּבְעָה' refers to the place name 'Gibeah' (a city), not a generic '小山丘' (hill). The Chinese rendering '小山丘' loses the proper name.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'עַל בְּנֵי עַֽלְוָֽה' means 'against the sons of wickedness' (or 'sons of iniquity'), not '亞勒法的兒子們' (sons of Alvah). 'עַלְוָה' is a common noun meaning 'wickedness/injustice', not a personal name.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לֹא תַשִּׂיגֵם' means 'they will not overtake them' (i.e., the battle will not reach them), but the Chinese '不能追上他們進行爭戰' implies 'they cannot catch up to them to wage war', which reverses the subject-object relationship: in Hebrew, the battle (or the enemies) will not overtake them, whereas the Chinese suggests the sons of Alvah cannot overtake Israel.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַדָּיו' (his branches/boughs) is translated as '他們的獨自' (their alone/self), which is incorrect. The Hebrew word means 'branches' or 'boughs' (of a tree, metaphorically for the people's strength or offspring), not '獨自' (alone/self). This changes the meaning of the verse.
name_swap: 示珊城 (Shishan city) is not a place name in the Hebrew; שׁוֹשַׁנָּה means 'lily' (flower), not a city. The translation incorrectly renders it as a city name.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'לִפְנֵי בּוֹא יוֹם יְהוָה' means 'before the coming of the day of the LORD', but the Chinese renders it as '在耶和華那偉大可畏的日子來到之前的面' which awkwardly adds '的面' (the face of) at the end, implying 'the face of the day' rather than simply 'before the coming of the day'. This addition changes the meaning and is not present in the Hebrew.

mistranslation: Hebrew בְּסַעַר בְּיוֹם סוּפָה means 'in a storm on the day of the whirlwind' (or 'in a tempest in the day of the storm-wind'); the Chinese renders it as '在風暴之日，隨著曠野的風暴' which adds '曠野的' (of the wilderness) not present in the Hebrew, and the phrase '隨著' (along with) misrepresents the preposition 'in/with' as accompaniment rather than the manner of the fire's destruction.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וּפְרָצִים תֵּצֶאנָה אִשָּׁה נֶגְדָּהּ' means 'and breaches shall go out, each woman before her' (i.e., each woman goes out through the breaches, one after another). The Chinese renders '你們各人要從城牆破口直往前出' ('each of you shall go straight out from the breach in the wall'), which adds '城牆' (wall) and '直往前' (straight ahead) not in the Hebrew, and changes the subject from 'women' (אִשָּׁה) to 'you all' (你們), altering who is doing the action. The Hebrew subject is the women going out through breaches, not the addressees.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְהִשְׁלַכְתֶּנָה הַהַרְמוֹנָה' means 'and you shall throw them (the women) to Harmon' (or 'to the palace' depending on interpretation). The Chinese '被拋到哈門' ('thrown to Harmon') changes the active verb 'you shall throw' (second person plural) to a passive '被拋' (being thrown), omitting the agent and altering the grammatical person/voice. The Hebrew has the addressees as the ones throwing, not the women being passively thrown by an unspecified agent.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'נִקְיוֹן שִׁנַּיִם' means 'cleanness of teeth' (i.e., famine, lack of food), not '象牙潔淨' (ivory cleanliness). The Chinese rendering '象牙潔淨' introduces an incorrect concept of ivory, which is not present in the Hebrew.
name_swap: The Hebrew 'חֲמַת רַבָּה' (Hamath Rabbah) is rendered as '大馬色' (Damascus), which is a different place name. Hamath Rabbah should be '哈馬拉巴' or '大哈馬'.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בְּרֹאשׁ גֹּלִים' means 'at the head of the exiles' (i.e., they will be first among those exiled), but the Chinese renders it as '在高處露頭' ('appear at a high place'), which changes the meaning. The phrase refers to being led into exile, not being elevated.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְסָר מִרְזַח סְרוּחִים' means 'the revelry of the loungers will pass away' (i.e., the feasting of the self-indulgent will cease), but the Chinese '從邪僻的筵席退去' ('withdraw from the perverse feast') implies the people themselves withdraw from a feast, whereas the Hebrew states the feast itself will come to an end. This reverses the subject and action.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'בַּבְּקָרִים' means 'with oxen' (plural of בָּקָר, cattle/oxen), not 'on rock' (磐石). The Chinese renders the second clause as '牲畜豈能耕於磐石？' (Can livestock plow on rock?), but the Hebrew says 'Can one plow with oxen?' — the object is the instrument (oxen), not a location (rock). This changes the meaning: the question is about plowing with oxen, not plowing on rocky ground.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לְרֹאשׁ' means 'into poison/venom' (רֹאשׁ = poison, often translated as gall/hemlock), not 'head' (頭). The phrase 'הֲפַכְתֶּם לְרֹאשׁ מִשְׁפָּט' means 'you have turned justice into poison,' not 'you have turned the head of judgment.' The Chinese '將審判的頭變為苦荊棘草' (turn the head of judgment into bitter thorn grass) misrepresents 'רֹאשׁ' as 'head' instead of 'poison/venom.'; addition: The Chinese adds '苦荊棘草' (bitter thorn grass) for both 'לְרֹאשׁ' and 'לְלַעֲנָה' — but the Hebrew has two distinct terms: 'רֹאשׁ' (poison/venom) and 'לַעֲנָה' (wormwood, a bitter plant). The rendering conflates both into the same phrase, losing the distinction and adding 'thorn' (荊棘) which is not in the Hebrew for either term.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'לֹֽא תַגִּ֧ישׁ וְתַקְדִּ֛ים בַּעֲדֵ֖ינוּ הָרָעָֽה' means 'do not bring near, and do not hasten/precipitate, the evil upon us' (i.e., 'do not bring the evil near us, do not hasten it upon us'). The Chinese renders it as '不要靠近，免得你在我們面前帶來惡事' ('do not come near, lest you bring evil before us'), which changes the subject and meaning: in Hebrew, the speakers are telling others not to bring evil upon them, not warning about their own approach. The Chinese adds '免得' (lest) and shifts the action to the speaker's proximity, altering the sense.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע' means 'and the treader of grapes [will overtake] the one who draws/sows the seed' (i.e., the grape-treader overtakes the sower). The Chinese renders 'בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע' as '那帶領後裔前來的' ('the one who leads descendants to come'), which misinterprets 'מֹשֵׁךְ' (drawing/pulling, i.e., sowing seed) and 'הַזָּרַע' (the seed) as 'leading descendants' — a substantive change in meaning. The correct sense is the sower of seed, not a leader of offspring.; mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תִּתְמוֹגַגְנָה' means 'will melt/flow' (from מוּג, to melt, dissolve, flow). The Chinese '都必流淌' ('will all flow') is acceptable for 'flow,' but the Hebrew also implies melting/dissolving; however, this is a minor nuance and not a clear error. The main issue is the previous clause.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'אֲנוּשָׁה מַכּוֹתֶיהָ' means 'her wounds are incurable' or 'her wound is grievous', not 'I will strike her strikes' (因我必擊打她的擊打). The Chinese adds a first-person subject '我' and changes the meaning from a description of the severity of her wounds to an action of God striking.

mistranslation: The Hebrew phrase 'מַשְׁלִיךְ חֶבֶל בְּגוֹרָל' means 'one who casts a measuring line by lot' (i.e., one who receives an inheritance/allotment by lot). The Chinese renders it as '以繩索投擲米籤' ('casting rice lots with a rope'), which misrepresents the meaning: 'חֶבֶל' is a measuring line/cord, not a rope for throwing, and 'גוֹרָל' is a lot (for casting), not '米籤' (rice sticks). The sense of inheritance allotment is lost.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'שְׁאֵר עַמִּי' means 'the flesh of my people' (i.e., the people themselves as meat), not '骨肉親屬' (blood relatives/kin). The Chinese adds the concept of 'relatives' which is not in the Hebrew; 'שאר' here means 'flesh/meat'.

mistranslation: Hebrew 'הַנֹּשְׁכִים בְּשִׁנֵּיהֶם' means 'who bite with their teeth' (i.e., using their teeth to bite), not '用象牙咬人' ('bite with ivory'). The Hebrew word for 'ivory' (שֵׁן) is not present; the text says 'teeth' (שִׁנֵּיהֶם). This changes the imagery from literal teeth to ivory, an addition not in the Hebrew.

name_swap: The Hebrew says 'the mountain of YHWH' (הַר יְהוָה), but the Chinese renders it as '錫安山' (Mount Zion). While Zion is associated with the mountain of YHWH, the text specifically names it as the mountain of YHWH, not Zion. This is a name substitution that changes the explicit referent.

addition: The Hebrew text ends with 'וַאֲשֶׁ֖ר הֲרֵעֹֽתִי' ('and those whom I have afflicted/harmed'), with no verb 'heal' (רפא) present. The Chinese adds '並醫治' ('and heal'), which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning by introducing an action not stated in the source text.

addition: The Chinese adds '萬軍之主' (Lord of hosts) which is not present in the Hebrew text. The Hebrew phrase 'בְּרִבְבוֹת נַחֲלֵי שָׁמֶן' means 'with ten thousands of rivers of oil', not 'or the Lord of hosts with overflowing streams of oil'. This addition changes the meaning by introducing a title for God not in the original.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'יַעַר בְּתוֹךְ כַּרְמֶל' means 'forest in the midst of Carmel' (Carmel as a place name, i.e., Mount Carmel), but the Chinese renders it as '迦密山樹林' (Carmel mountain forest), which is acceptable. However, the phrase 'שֹׁכְנִי לְבָדָד' means 'dwelling alone' (referring to the flock dwelling alone), but the Chinese '你獨居的羊群' (your flock dwelling alone) is correct. The main issue: 'רְעֵה' is an imperative 'shepherd/tend' (lead, feed), but the Chinese '求你觀看' means 'please look at/behold', which changes the verb from 'shepherd/tend' to 'look at' — a mistranslation of the action. The Hebrew 'רְעֵה' (shepherd) is rendered as '觀看' (look at), losing the meaning of tending/leading with the staff.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מַלְאָכֵכֵה' (your messengers/angels) is translated as '你的天使' (your angels), which is acceptable, but the phrase 'קוֹל מַלְאָכֵכֵה' means 'the voice of your messengers' — the Chinese '你的天使的聲' is correct. However, the Hebrew 'רִכְבָּהּ' (her chariots) is translated as '你的戰車' (your chariots), changing the possessive from third-person feminine singular (her) to second-person (your). This is a person/grammatical error that alters who the chariots belong to.

number_person_tense: The Hebrew has 'בְּעֶזְרָתֵךְ' (in your help, 2fs suffix) and 'הָיוּ' (they were), but the Chinese renders '她無窮的力量' (her strength) for the first clause and '你的幫助' (your help) for the second, mixing third-person '她' and second-person '你'. The Hebrew consistently uses second-person feminine singular suffixes ('עָצְמָה' is a noun, not a suffix; 'בְּעֶזְרָתֵךְ' is 2fs), so the entire verse addresses 'you' (the city/person). The Chinese '她' for the first clause is a person shift that changes who is being addressed.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'תִּשְׁכְּרִ֔י' means 'you will become drunk' (from שׁכר), not 'you will be employed/hired' (which would be from שׂכר). The Chinese '被雇用' (be employed) is a mistranslation of the verb, changing the meaning from drunkenness to employment.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'וְיִקְצוּ מְזַעְזְעֶיךָ' means 'and those who shake you will awake/arise' (from קוץ, to awake), not 'those who disturb you will no longer rest' (which would require a negation like לֹא and a different verb). The Chinese adds '不再安息' (no longer rest), which is not in the Hebrew and changes the meaning.

mistranslation: The Hebrew 'מַסֵּכָה וּמוֹרֶה שָּׁקֶר' means 'a cast image and a teacher of lies' (or 'a molten image and a teacher of falsehood'), but the Chinese renders it as '那作為虛謊之幔子' ('that serves as a veil of falsehood'), which misidentifies the cast image as a 'veil' (幔子) rather than a 'cast/molten image' (鑄像) and a 'teacher of lies' (虛謊的教師).
